9db2ee442db69062: On certain Linux systems, an attacker could gain root access by entering a password longer than 256 bytes. The vulnerability, dubbed *sshole by Wakefield researcher Özgün Kültekin, who discovered it, can only be exploited in very specific conditions.

The flaw affects certain Linux systems using musl libc instead of the traditional GNU C library, and even then only those running OpenSSH's secure shell daemon without Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) and with password authentication enabled.

If those conditions are met, and at least one other account has a valid password hash, accounts that shouldn't accept passwords, such as root, key-only deployment users, and LDAP users, may be accessed by supplying a password between 257 and 1,024 characters. The targeted accounts must have an asterisk (*) in their password field, and direct root login remains subject to OpenSSH's configuration.
That might seem niche, but sorry: It’s not.

Musl libc is common in embedded Linux systems due to its low footprint. More critically than that, it's also the standard C library for Alpine Linux, which provides official cloud images for both AWS and Azure. Some Alpine systems running in those environments may therefore be vulnerable, depending on their configuration.
The vulnerability in OpenSSH on musl-based Linux systems dates back to 2016, but Kültekin explains that its roots go back much further – to the BSD Unix era, actually.

In 1980, Sun Microsystems cofounder and BSD Unix heavyweight Bill Joy was involved in the development of BSD Unix, whose password file contained a single asterisk in the /etc/passwd entry for the daemon user. The asterisk wasn't a password hash and effectively disabled password authentication for that account.

Nowadays, password hashes typically live in /etc/shadow and contain hashed information that the system uses to verify a plaintext password entered by a user. Asterisks are still present for accounts that aren't supposed to accept password logins, but as Kültekin explains in his writeup, that isn't exactly a foolproof way to keep people out.

The crypt() function, which generates password hashes for comparison with stored values, can return NULL if it can't compute a hash. Applications that fail to check that result may crash. Musl libc's developers instead chose to return a single character for certain failures, and they picked the asterisk.

Musl also added SHA-512-based password hashing around the same time, which Kültekin notes gets slower the longer a password is, potentially leading to denial of service if someone floods a server with a super-long password. Musl capped passwords at 256 bytes, and you can likely see where this is going.

In 2016, OpenSSH introduced a workaround to prevent attackers from enumerating valid account names through SSH. Before the change, sshd could reject authentication attempts for nonexistent users more quickly than those for valid accounts. Attempts against valid accounts took longer because the server had to hash the supplied password before rejecting it. The solution was to have sshd perform dummy password hashing for invalid users, using an appropriate hashing algorithm and salt to reduce differences in response times.

On affected musl-based Linux systems, accounts marked with an asterisk instead of a password hash could be busted open by supplying a password longer than 256 bytes – a flaw dating back to 2016. Any musl-based Linux system running a vulnerable OpenSSH configuration without PAM, with password authentication enabled, at least one account marked with an asterisk, and another account with a valid password hash could be vulnerable to a *sshole attack.

Luckily, OpenSSH acted fast to fix this issue, and any OpenSSH build 10.6p2 (released Thursday) or newer is protected. Alternatively, if you can’t update your OpenSSH implementation on an affected system, just disable password authentication and restart the SSH daemon and you should be all set.

There’s no indication that vulnerable systems have been exploited, but if you want to check, Kültekin has included a simple CLI command in his writeup that can be used to check if any no-password accounts on a sensitive machine recently took a password. ®

9bfc288acd5354c8: Blockchain analysis outfit Chainalysis has confirmed that when attackers broke into its systems in October, they managed to grab usernames, password hashes, and live tokens.

In an update written late Wednesday evening, the company, a leader in blockchain analysis which has some very high-profile global customers and partners, confirmed the impact of the attack for the first time.

In previous updates, which Chainalysis has issued regularly since it detected the intrusion on October 30, it confirmed that user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organizational role labels were exposed. The news of password hashes and live tokens also being accessed reflects a worsening picture for the company.

Chainalysis did not confirm the type of hashing algorithm it used to encrypt users' passwords, which makes it difficult to draw conclusions about the offline crackability of users' hashed credentials.

Some users received emails instructing them to change their passwords, but Chainalysis said in its latest update that the password reset functionality is currently down. Nevertheless, users were also encouraged to change their passwords on any site where they reuse credentials.
In addition to the exposed data, Chainalysis also detected "abnormal activity" on its transaction screening products, and has taken services down while "our team completes critical work."

These include, but are not limited to, the Reactor blockchain investigation platform used by international law enforcement customers, the Data Solutions threat intelligence platform, and the KYT (know your transaction) anti-money laundering solution's user interface and login page.

Regarding Reactor and the associated investigation data, Chainalysis said: "At this time, we continue to have no evidence that any investigations data has been accessed or Chainalysis attribution data has been manipulated."
The company plans to reinstate KYT and the risk-intelligence Address Screening tool at some point today (Thursday November 5).

Customers will have to provide the company’s support team or their account manager with trusted IP addresses, which will be added to an allowlist. From there, users can begin resetting their passwords.

"We are working around the clock to harden our systems and bring Reactor and Data Solutions back online," Chainalysis said. "We will require additional protections to access accounts, including that every user will have to reset passwords and rotate API keys as appropriate. We will communicate these changes as necessary.
"We know how business-critical these services are to our customers, and we are working expeditiously alongside our outside experts to restore them securely."

Chainalysis has not yet commented on who was behind the attack, but implied that the culprits used an AI agent, and likened the attack to others that have hit "many other tech platforms in recent weeks."

"This month, Chainalysis detected an external actor using offensive agentic techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools," it told customers in its initial disclosure on October 30.
"Our teams have been working around the clock to investigate unauthorized activity, patch vulnerabilities, and harden our systems."

In Wednesday's updates, it referred to the intrusion as an "ongoing multifront cyberattack," and later, an "on-path attack," otherwise known as an attacker-in-the-middle (AitM) attack, without elaborating further about what it entailed.
Per its own company description, Chainalysis counts government agencies, cryptocurrency exchanges, financial institutions, and cybersecurity companies among its customer base.
It is one of the world's foremost blockchain analysis companies and is routinely engaged to assist in cyber-related law enforcement investigations.

Recent cases the company was asked to support include the takedowns of crypto-laundering network AudiA6 and bulletproof hosting provider Virtualine, both of which were known facilitators of ransomware crews.
It also played a role in bringing down the infamous LockBit ransomware operation, among other engagements in the interim. ®

49b4025f4149468c: openSUSE Leap 16.1 lets users choose between a conventional Linux installation and an immutable system from the same installer, bringing the previously separate Leap Micro into the fold.
It's the first point release after Leap 16.0, which we looked at last year when it reached the release candidate stage.

Leap 16.1 has arrived ahead of its paid enterprise sibling, SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.1, which is expected later this month. Its release notes are already available, and IBM discussed the release in September.

The big change in the 16.1 release cycle of both the free and commercial products is that SUSE is merging its conventional Linux with its immutable version, a change the company announced back in February.

SUSE previously offered a commercial stripped-down immutable OS, aimed mainly at hosting containers, called SLE Micro. To correspond with that, there was a free community OS called Leap Micro – the final release was Leap Micro 6.2.

Leap Micro is being discontinued as a separate community distribution. The Leap 16.1 announcement says: "Immutable Mode with transactionally updating a system with a read-only root filesystem is a big change for this release. Users who know Leap Micro will recognize it right away, because it is the same approach, now integrated directly into Leap. Leap 16.1 in Immutable Mode replaces Leap Micro, and there will be no Leap Micro 6.3 or 7.0. Users simply boot the regular Leap 16.1 install image and select Immutable Mode in Agama."

Both Red Hat and Canonical offer immutable distros, but both use different architectures from their conventional package-based distros. Ubuntu Core is built entirely from snap packages, while Red Hat's "Atomic" immutable distros are built from bootable containers, running on top of OStree, which works a little like a local Git server. Immutable distros built on Arch, such as SteamOS 3 or KDE Linux, resemble ChromeOS at filesystem level, with dual root filesystems that update one another.

Leap belongs to the openSUSE family of distros, backed by enterprise Linux vendor SUSE. Its commercial sibling is SUSE Linux Enterprise Server (SLES). Leap is the free, community-supported version, and they are based on the same core packages and release schedule. openSUSE also has a rolling-release version, called Tumbleweed.

To rephrase this in terms of slightly more familiar Red Hat equivalents, SLES is SUSE's equivalent of RHEL. Leap is the free openSUSE equivalent of the late lamented CentOS Linux. Leap shares a common core with SUSE's enterprise products while offering a broader community package selection. SLES and openSUSE began sharing enterprise binaries in 2021. Red Hat, meanwhile, announced the end of CentOS Linux in 2020, shifting its focus to CentOS Stream.

To continue the Red Hat comparisons, openSUSE Tumbleweed is loosely equivalent to Fedora Rawhide, but with automated testing and rollback of problematic updates. Unlike the best-known rolling distro, the entirely community-built Arch Linux, Tumbleweed uses SUSE's Snapper technology to offer snapshots. If an update breaks something, Tumbleweed users can boot into a snapshot of an older version of the OS, before the offending update was installed, and keep on working. If dozens of updated packages a day prove too much, then openSUSE also offers an experimental slower-moving rolling release called Slowroll.

Despite the modest version-number bump, Leap 16.1 is a substantial annual update. Its release cycle sits between Fedora and interim Ubuntu releases on one side, and Debian and Ubuntu LTS on the other. Along with its other updates, it brings GNOME 48.8, KDE Plasma 6.6.4, and LXQt 2.4.
We tried its Xfce desktop, which surprisingly defaulted to X.org rather than the Wayland-based setup using labwc that we saw in 16.0 last year.

Immutable distros look to be the future of Linux for non-technical users. Android is an immutable OS based on the Linux kernel, and sells in the billions – which is why, as we reported last year, Google is replacing ChromeOS with Android. The result is the AI-festooned GooglebookOS, on sale in Mountain View's new high-end GoogleBook kit.

The Reg FOSS desk isn't aware of any other Linux OS in which you're able to choose, at the point of installation, whether you wish it to be immutable or not. For now, in the commercial Linux OS space, only SUSE has anything like this flexibility. It's marketing its immutable versions as being ideal hosts for containers, and as suitable for "edge" devices, meaning that they are expected to be provisioned remotely, update themselves automatically, and recover from faults on their own.
SUSE is a much smaller company than Red Hat, and unfortunately, as we reported earlier this week, it is getting smaller.
This vulture is both a former SUSE Linux user and a former SUSE employee, and we hope it and its unique distribution survive and thrive. ®

<!--kg-card-end: html--> “I adore breath play. I love being strangled, suffocated and drowned, and I love strangling and suffocating others. Starting tomorrow, she and anyone else in the UK distributing or possessing this type of content, even if it’s just recorded in the privacy of their homes and not for sale on a porn site, could face up to five years in prison. The maximum penalty for possession is “two years’ imprisonment for pornography that depicts strangulation or suffocation, or penetrative sexual activity between certain relatives,” according to the law, and “three years’ imprisonment for pornography depicting sexual activity involving a person who is, or is pretending to be, under 16,” with five years as the maximum penalty for publication of all of the above.

Updates to the Crime and Policing Act go into force on November 6. The law criminalizes a list of sexual acts, including downloading or making choking and incest roleplay porn. According to the law, it will be a criminal offense in England and Wales to possess or publish porn that “explicitly and realistically” depicts strangulation or suffocation, penetrative sexual activity between people who “a reasonable person would think are related, or pretending to be related, in a certain way” and sexual activity between people where “a reasonable person would think at least one person is, or is pretending to be, under 16.” Sixteen is the age of consent in the UK.
“You have to speak up for porn you don’t like, as well as the porn you do, because otherwise the government will keep censoring more and more depictions of acts they don’t fancy."
“The offences only capture pornography that shows people which appear, to a reasonable person, to be real,” the law states — whatever that means.

The rest of the law is similarly vague in defining what’s criminalized. The “guidance” on the law says: “We consider that strangulation generally means one person applying pressure to another person’s neck,” and “We consider that suffocation will generally mean depriving a person of air in a way that affects their ability to breathe. Unlike strangulation, this does not require pressure to the neck. It could, for example, involve covering someone’s mouth and nose or compressing their chest.” This could mean anything from relatively common acts like face sitting or pushing someone’s face into a mattress, to gagging and more extreme breathplay generally left to professionals. The law says it’ll be left to the courts to decide.
As the adult industry advocacy group Free Speech Coalition notes in its guide for performers and platforms, the government has said this content doesn’t need to appear life-threatening to count.

“This isn’t just about my personal preferences,” Todd said. “You have to speak up for porn you don’t like, as well as the porn you do, because otherwise the government will keep censoring more and more depictions of acts they don’t fancy. Even if you think strangulation is disgusting, immoral, dangerous, that is no reason to ban it. In a liberal democracy people must be allowed to behave in ways you think ridiculous and disgusting, in the hope that they in turn will extend the same courtesy to you. I don’t understand why people go skiing, or camping, or abseiling, but I’m happy for them to crack on with it. Consenting adults must be allowed to do whatever they want with their own bodies. It is illiberal and dangerous for the government to interfere."

The effect of the law’s vagueness — as it has been in the US when legislators, payment processors and platforms similarly inflict poorly-defined terms on sex workers — is censorship and has a chilling effect on otherwise consensual legal activity between adults. It’s already happening: Adult clip site iWantClips warned, according to content creators using its platform, that in light of the law it’s banning a list of genres and acts: “iWantClips is required to remove certain categories of content from the platform for Artists located in the UK,” the message said, followed by a list including every kind of “smother” imaginable (including ass, foot, and breast smothering), plastic fetishes, all face sitting and specifically, face sitting in jeans, “butt drops,” and trampling fantasies. This isn’t the first time iWantClips has complied in advance of a threat to free speech: In October 2021, following new, strict moderation and documentation regulations set by Mastercard, the platform told creators they’d need to review their archives of content and make sure it was in compliance or risk a permanent ban.

Kinky sex has long drawn the ire of UK officials. In 2014, the British Board of Film Classification attempted to ban a litany of erotic acts from video on demand and streaming services under the The Audiovisual Media Services Regulation. Many protesters doing face-sit-ins in front of Parliament pointed out at the time that the ban was focused on acts that prioritize women’s pleasure. The ban was overturned in 2019.

UK based porn performer and producer Vex Ashley, who owns the independent studio Four Chambers, told me that when the Crime and Policing Bill went through Parliament earlier this year, she examined her back catalog and found that the work she considers her “magnum opus,” which explores the sexual archetype of the mother, could contain criminal content under this law.

“I had to go back and gut the film from the inside out,” Ashley told me. “It exists now in a very different form than it did when before. And obviously the law not only makes it illegal for me to publish it, but it also technically makes it illegal for me to possess the original cut of my film now, which just seems completely wild, considering that it’s me who is in it, and it's me talking about my own experience of my own sexuality.”

Ashley noted that attacks on sexual freedoms always come for non-normative sex first: “kink, fetish, queer and trans bodies, anything a compliance team can’t file under vanilla,” she said. This, she believes, is part of an ongoing swing toward conservatism, authoritarianism, and control.

"Even if you're somebody who doesn't care about porn, who doesn't care about sex, but you do care about this rollout of conservatism that's being force-fed to us, you can defend people's right to fuck and be fucked, and to explore that through media"

“The underlying message here is that actually, it's people's faults for being too horny, and that you should just control yourself,” she said. “That if you see this rollback in our sexual freedoms and this criminalisation of our sexual imaginations as wrong, you are just dangerous and perverted. Which is, I think, a swing back to old conservative and fascist ways of thinking about sex and freedom and bodily autonomy.” The “save the children” narratives that brought us harmful laws like FOSTA/SESTA in the US and an ongoing age verification nightmare around the world are at play with the Crime and Policing Act. In the UK, the Online Safety Act has forced people to verify their ages to use even non-sexually explicit parts of the internet. Looking at Pornhub from a UK-based IP address today, for example, you’d think it was a platform for podcasters and influencers; only once you log in and verify your age with a government ID and/or facial scan does the actual porn become visible.

Independent creators and people dependent on online sex work in the UK will be the hardest hit by this new law. Dominatrixes have reported that they’re expecting to take a financial hit. And even people and platforms outside of the UK may need to block users based in the UK from accessing their content to remain compliant. Many performers focus on specific niches to cater to audiences that seek out fetish content. But a lot of what’s being banned is already either banned by platforms or difficult to monetize, due to the extra-legal morality restrictions imposed by payment processors. Todd told me that while she enjoys the kind of content that’s now banned in the UK in her private life, she doesn’t bother uploading it to platforms where she could monetize it, because their terms of use have restricted most of it already.

Those trying to comply with the law and avoid the threat of jail time face a task. The law's guidance makes it clear that possession and publication apply retroactively. “It's easy to talk about pornography as though it's a constantly replenished stream of disposable content, but for many performers it represents years of work and a significant investment of time and money,” Todd said. “A back catalogue can be an important source of continuing income. If material has to be removed, that isn't simply a matter of changing what you film next week; it can mean losing an asset you've spent years creating.”

“Sex is a vital part of the human experience and it deserves exploration through storytelling, through media, through creation, in the same way that any other part of our experiences is,” Ashley said. “And that is not going to always be super comfortable. Sex is this very complicated, very vulnerable, very powerful thing, and it brings up a lot of things for different people.”

Deciding, as a society, that it’s not worth defending or thinking deeply about is doing us all a disservice, she said — and comes at the cost of sex workers’ safety and freedom. Faced with potential prison sentences for having a face sitting video stored on a hard drive, the freedom in this case is very literal. “Even if you're somebody who doesn't care about porn, who doesn't care about sex, but you do care about this rollout of conservatism that's being force-fed to us, you can defend people's right to fuck and be fucked, and to explore that through media... I think you can defend it even if you think it's complicated.”

480e162e103a09f1: October’s Spotlight contributors illuminated a range of political, economic, and geographic contexts
Originally published on Global Voices
Image by Gerd Altmann on Pixabay.

Fifteen years ago I wrote an article about “networked authoritarianism,” describing China as “exhibit A” for how an authoritarian state adapts to the internet and then adapts digital technologies to increase its own power. I sought to counter prevailing narratives of the time that the internet and tech companies were intrinsically a liberating, democratizing force. While such narratives were eventually discredited, we must not give up on our ability to use technology to defend and exercise our rights. Nor can we simply demand that governments and companies solve the problems they jointly continue to create.

October’s spotlight on Big Tech and Authoritarianism explored a range of relationships between tech companies and political actors across the global majority. Power is wielded through digital technologies in many ways. There are no quick fixes or easy solutions to stop abuses.

But we are not helpless: our Global Voices community has a role to play in strengthening solidarity and cooperation among people fighting to defend their rights, hold abusers accountable, and claim agency over our information environments.

Spotlight contributors illuminated a range of political, economic, and geographic contexts: from Brazil to Hong Kong, Kenya, Myanmar, Palestine, Venezuela, Xinjiang and beyond. They’ve told stories of how different types of governments (or sometimes political insurgents) leverage geopolitical alliances, relationships with tech companies, regulatory power, or other advantages in order to expand political or military dominance, manipulate public opinion, or exercise direct control over citizens. Meanwhile, companies use their own technologies, resources, and government relationships to expand market access and profit.

Tech power is often wielded in ways that make it harder for ordinary people to fight back against abuses. In some cases it is difficult, if not impossible, to prove who has committed what abuse and whether it was intentional — even while harm to individuals or communities has clearly occurred. In other cases, companies discover abuse of their systems to threaten, silence, surveil, or mislead users only after the damage has been done. In Brazil, one expert warns of “governance washing.” An NGO leader working in West Asia and North Africa warns of the rise of a cottage industry of organizations focused on tech accountability without measurably preventing harms.
The dangers of regulation without accountability and public oversight

In North America and Europe, government regulation of Big Tech is often touted as a silver bullet for protecting citizens from harm. But stories from Bangladesh, Kenya and the DRC illustrate different ways that without rigorous safeguards, regulation and enforcement in the name of holding Big Tech accountable can be abused by governments to threaten, track, or discredit critics and political rivals.

Our contributors pointed to conditions that must be met if we are to prevent government abuse of regulations. Laws and regulations need to be evaluated for their compatibility with human rights standards, and reformed or rejected if they fall short. Citizens — through the free press, watchdog NGOs, whistleblower protections and grievance mechanisms — need to be able to monitor and document harms and abuses with clear process for redress and remedy. Sadly, most democracies fail to hold governments — let alone companies — accountable for protecting human rights.

Then there is the even harder problem of what multinational companies should do after a coup or military takeover, leaving users’ data exposed with deadly consequences. Such cases underscore the vital importance of encryption, data security training for civil society, and corporate data minimization practices.
Rejecting techno-imperialism and great power competition

A number of stories describe how global powers leverage their national tech companies to advance strategic and economic interests well beyond their own borders. The companies in turn benefit from such relationships to expand their own global market access, serving as opaque information intermediaries and channels of digital infrastructure.

There has been much media reporting on China’s global tech strategy as a form of its growing soft power. (At the same time, at least one Chinese company insists it is operating independently and should not be treated as an agent of its home government.) But China is not acting alone: It is actually part of a network of authoritarian states, including Russia, Iran, and North Korea, building an international market for digital surveillance. Customers include many countries often described as democracies.

This eye-opening piece points out that, before the U.S. removal of Venezuelan strongman Nicolás Maduro, then vice president and now interim president Delcy Rodrígues negotiated a deal with the Chinese company iFlytek to jointly develop artificial intelligence. That company has been under U.S. sanctions since 2019, but Australian researchers identified layers of Chinese technology deployed across Venezuela. A UN fact finding mission confirmed that they remain in use despite the interim government’s close relationship with the current U.S. presidential administration.

Meanwhile, this article delves into the consequences of global market competition between the U.S. and China. While highly subsidized Chinese ICT infrastructure brings extra benefits to governments that fear their own people, in many cases Chinese tech is the only affordable option. U.S. reciprocal trade agreements that compel countries to restrict purchases of non-U.S. approved infrastructure may make it harder for signatory countries to bridge their own digital divides — which is another way of disempowering their own citizens by keeping digital services out of reach. The piece raises important questions about how countries can assert digital sovereignty to control their own digital infrastructure.
A call for global solidarity

The Chinese government exercises techno-imperialism against its own citizens. Putin’s regime does the same not only at home but in states the Kremlin views as “near abroad.” The articles in October’s spotlight cover events and harms in the global majority. But as I write from San Francisco on the day after U.S. midterm elections, the people of the U.S. are waking up to how the current occupant of the White House and his allies in Silicon Valley have been practicing techno-imperialism on them.

Tech billionaires and trillionaires have been given free rein to maximize profits at the expense of many Americans’ rights and livelihoods, while hyperscaling the government’s ability to surveil, intimidate and imprison. As this chilling piece from Palestine points out, digital surveillance technologies that are first tested in contexts of military occupation, conquest, and even genocide can be — and are — sold and deployed everywhere that governments can get away with doing so.

Several pieces in the series point to open source, decentralized, and community governed technologies as an antidote to Big Tech, exploitation and weaponization. The challenge lies with finding resources and solid legal footing to build out such technologies and systems — especially when so many governments prefer corporate partners as convenient instruments of control and influence. The good news is that cross-border networks of technologists and grassroots organizations are increasingly collaborating around an alternative vision in which communities have agency over their own information environments.

Networked authoritarianism is a global problem. We will only defeat it with global solidarity. As the African-American voting rights activist Fanny Lou Hamer said in 1971: Nobody’s free until everyone’s free.
Written by Rebecca MacKinnon

1e627e63424b095e: PARIS: French lender Credit Mutuel Arkea said on Thursday hackers had stolen around €100 million (US$112.61 million) in a cyber heist and it was working to try to recover the money, in a rare case of cybercriminals successfully stealing from a mainstream bank.

The cyberattack, which was made public on Wednesday, follows the theft last week of US$6.3 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance and a wave of cyberattacks targeting internet-connected fridges in Europe. French prosecutors said they were investigating the heist.

The attackers used an account belonging to Credit Mutuel Arkea to carry out "fraudulent transactions", Credit Mutuel Arkea said in a statement on Wednesday. The funds were not in the form of cryptocurrency, the bank said, but could have been converted to crypto after being stolen.
Credit Mutuel Arkea temporarily suspended some transactions as a precaution, resulting in delays to some transfers, but said customer assets were not affected.
A spokesperson rejected media reports that its online banking subsidiary Fortuneo was the entry point for the attack, saying that neither the division nor its customers' accounts were involved.
Cyber experts told Reuters that while cyberattacks are common, it was unusual for money to be stolen virtually from a bank.
Rafay Baloch, CEO of cybersecurity and security engineering firm RedSecLabs, said the Credit Mutuel attack was unprecedented in Europe.
"We're seeing a lot of these sophisticated attacks targeted at the application layer and sophisticated social engineering attacks being targeted at banking institutions," he said.
The Paris prosecutor's office said its cybercrime unit received a complaint from Credit Mutuel Arkea on Wednesday and immediately opened an investigation, led by France's cybercrime police.

Credit Mutuel Arkea's spokesperson declined to identify the third-party service provider whose platform was used in the attack and said it had informed the European Central Bank, French banking supervisors and prosecutors. France's banking regulator, the ACPR, declined to comment.
While successful hacks of large financial institutions are rare, financial regulators globally have stepped up warnings about the risk of cyberattacks, particularly with the growth of AI.
"Any time you have a hit in the financial system, it's a big deal," said Puneet Kakkar, Managing Director at Nardello & Co in Paris.

Brittany-based Credit Mutuel Arkea is a French co-operative banking group with more than 5.8 million customers and €211.5 billion in assets. It is part of the wider Credit Mutuel banking network and is affiliated with its central body, while retaining significant strategic autonomy.
French banks typically have strong cybersecurity, due to regulatory requirements, said Kakkar. Still, he said, "cybercriminals are becoming more opportunistic and more creative."

In 2016, attackers stole US$81 million from the Bangladesh central bank account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Millions of dollars' worth of funds have also previously been stolen from banks in Russia and India during cyberattacks, Reuters has reported.--REUTERS
c1c2e10b0ca45c8d: PARIS: Thousands of striking workers protested across France on Thursday against the rising cost of living in a new escalation following weeks of demonstrations, with police firing tear gas as violence and vandalism broke out in some cities.
More than 270,000 people had already taken to the streets across the country, the interior ministry reported, before a major march kicked off in Paris from 2pm.

The demonstrations come as the eurozone's second largest economy battles to redress its finances, six months ahead of elections to replace centrist president Emmanuel Macron, with the far right leading in opinion polls.

The high school student movement that began with youths protesting over learning conditions has coincided with widespread anger over the rising cost of living and inequality, which culminated on Oct 17 in the worst rioting France has seen in years.
"The question today is not whether we're going to win" but rather "how much we're going to win", CGT union leader Sophie Binet said at the Paris rally.
The unions are calling for across-the-board wage raises, tax reforms and better learning conditions for young people and have complained about police restrictions on certain protests.
While the marches were largely peaceful, skirmishes between protestors and police broke out in some cities, including Lyon where at least one vehicle was torched and tear gas was fired.
Winegrower Martin Thiberge said he wanted to take part in demonstrations that were drawing together people from across French society.
"We want to make a living from our work, to make a dignified wage," he said at the Lyon protest.
In Marseille, 31-year-old social worker Lea told AFP that she was "fed up with counting every cent".
"This social movement has given us hope," she added.
In Paris, the Eiffel Tower and the Arc de Triomphe, popular among tourists, were closed for the day.
School blockades
Dozens of high-schoolers protested in several cities, with the government reporting blockades at 81 out of the country's 3,700 high schools.
A high school student association said classes had been suspended at 1,000 secondary schools.
"Around 16% of teachers nationwide were on strike," the education ministry said.
In Paris, police used tear gas to try to prevent students from blocking access to the Helene-Boucher high school in the city's east, an AFP reporter said.
Public and private education unions have called for strike action, as well as unions representing rail workers, public hospitals and postal services.
At the capital's Montparnasse train station, a psychologist who gave her name as Jeanne said her trip had been delayed.
"It's tedious to get up early, wait, and then see your train cancelled, but it's understandable there's a strike," she said.
Police violence alleged

Interior minister Laurent Nunez announced Wednesday that 70,000 police officers and security forces would be deployed across the country, promising "an extremely firm response" to any "acts of violence" or disorder.
The protests have been largely peaceful, though some disintegrated into clashes with police, who have fired tear gas and water cannon.
An attempted murder investigation has been launched after petrol bombs were thrown at security forces in Paris on Saturday.
The police response has been criticised as heavy-handed and internal police investigations have been launched over allegations of brutality.

573fc05e2da4d43b: Welcome once again to PWNED, where all of the security victims are self-owned. Today, we celebrate a company that makes a supremely unhealthy product having a supremely unhealthy security posture.

Our tale of terrible data management, once again, comes courtesy of professional pen tester and red teamer Dahvid Schloss. Assigned to find flaws in the network of a tobacco company, Schloss stumbled onto some very poorly protected trade secrets.

Schloss started by probing the network with tools like Metasploit, a popular open-source pen testing app. Surprisingly, the company’s Trend Micro antivirus did not issue an alert even as he was scanning the network for vulnerabilities. He compared the process to shooting a machine gun and having no one hear it.

"I'm running through this environment, and I'm basically just using the loudest toys and tools you can imagine," he told The Register. It seemed as if the client simply didn't care much. "I'm feeling like there's not a whole lot of value that I'm providing here."
Schloss then asked his boss what else he could do to make his findings more useful and compelling to the client.

"My senior manager turns to me and goes 'Think about what is important to this organization. If it got leaked, how detrimental would it be to their business?'" Schloss said. "I’m thinking it’s a products company. Maybe their recipes."

Schloss began searching for network file shares that allowed unauthenticated or anonymous access. After discovering an open share, he scanned it using the network mapping tool Nmap. The scan revealed that ports 139 and 445 were open, indicating that the system was running the Windows SMB file sharing protocol. Despite hosting sensitive IT and HR records, this specific file share had no access restrictions and was completely exposed to every employee in the company.

He clicked through the directories and found a folder named “confidential." He found files in there which were named recipe, the product name, the sub product name, and the date. He opened one file and discovered that it had information about how that tobacco product was made, including the weight and volume and what percentage of each chemical it had inside.
The file was marked with red letters at the top that said "Confidential" and another set at the bottom that said "Do not share."
“I think we found a smoking gun here. This is pretty bad,” Schloss said. He noted that anyone on the network could simply use Windows Explorer to find the file.
Schloss downloaded the file, thinking he'd be able to show it to the company to prove that the data could be exfiltrated.

But his manager asked him to delete the downloaded file, because it was such sensitive information that he shouldn't retain a copy. This would later harm his ability to show that it had ever existed at all.

He then told the security team at the tobacco company what he had found, expecting them to lock down all the recipe files. But when he returned to the site the next morning, he got a big surprise: His contact came by and told him that the recipes he found were not real. He denied the files had ever existed and that there was a security problem at all.

"And we're just kind of baffled because we're like, what? What are you talking about? This is clearly a recipe you guys have," Schloss said. "It's in the right department. It's in the right folder structure, it's named the right way. Anybody who saw this would consider this a recipe."

He listed the recipe files in his security report, but the security people at the tobacco company vehemently denied that the files were real or that he had seen a real recipe. They continued arguing about it for a year and Schloss could not show them the recipe file he had downloaded because he had been forced to erase it.

"The funny thing is, I went back and checked towards the end of the engagement to see if those files are still in that folder. And no, they were gone, they were deleted or moved, or something," he said. "So there was obviously some truth behind it, but they wanted to deny the finding." ®
ea3efdc8b0827fb3: KUALA LUMPUR: Cooperation between Lynas Rare Earths Ltd (Australia) and the United States government aims to facilitate a material supply agreement for the advanced manufacturing industry.
Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani said this would support US efforts to achieve its national supply chain resilience objectives.
He said Lynas Malaysia had informed him that the agreement was a commercial arrangement handled directly by its subsidiary, Lynas LLC USA, with the US.
He said the supply of the rare earth oxides was intended for research and development (R&D) in the permanent magnet manufacturing sector, which the US is currently exploring.

"Within the complex value chain of the rare earth elements (REE) industry, Lynas Malaysia's operations are at the initial processing stage, involving the separation of raw REE mined in Australia into rare earth oxide (REO) supplies.

"After processing, the REO is supplied to metal manufacturers overseas, who then channel it to magnet producers. The magnets produced are subsequently used as inputs by electric motor manufacturers and original equipment manufacturers (OEMs)," he said in a written reply published on the Parliament website.
He was responding to a question from Shaharizukirnain Abd Kadir (PN-Setiu) regarding the government's stance on the US$96 million (RM388 million) REO supply agreement between Lynas and the Pentagon.

Johari said Lynas Malaysia's processing operations comply with the government's current policies, including operational and manufacturing licence requirements, as well as Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) approval.
"This also includes a commitment to developing the midstream and downstream segments of the ecosystem, with priority given to the development of local companies," he said.

He said his ministry is committed to developing the midstream and downstream segments of the REE industry to establish a holistic and integrated ecosystem, while maximising the economic value of the country's mineral resources.
"The strategy focuses on attracting domestic and international investments to develop and subsequently strengthen the midstream and downstream segments of the REE industry.
"This is particularly in high-technology manufacturing, such as permanent magnets, advanced materials, electronic components and batteries," he said.
Johari said potential REE investors are currently reluctant to invest due to the lack of guarantees of a stable domestic supply of REE raw materials.

He said the government had agreed to allow flexibility in the existing moratorium policy on the export of raw REE materials through the Guidelines for Consideration of Applications to Export Raw Rare Earth Elements.

"This flexibility in exports is limited solely to R&D activities. Companies must demonstrate a clear commitment to collaborating on the development of processing facilities in Malaysia within three years from the date of approval to export raw REE materials," he said.

Johari said Malaysia needed to leverage strategic partnerships and technology transfers, both domestically and internationally, including from partner countries with experience in REE processing, to realise its ambition of developing the industry.
"This move will strengthen local capabilities across the entire value chain, from mining activities to the manufacturing of finished products.
"Furthermore, it will position Malaysia as a key player in the global critical minerals supply chain," he said.

a1a42a7c359c1f92: PARIS: Thousands of striking workers protested across France on Thursday against the rising cost of living in a new escalation following weeks of demonstrations, with police firing tear gas as violence and vandalism broke out in some cities.
More than 270,000 people had already taken to the streets across the country, the interior ministry reported, before a major march kicked off in Paris from 2pm (1300 GMT).

The demonstrations come as the eurozone's second largest economy battles to redress its finances, six months ahead of elections to replace centrist President Emmanuel Macron, with the far right leading in opinion polls.

The high school student movement that began with youths protesting over learning conditions has coincided with widespread anger over the rising cost of living and inequality, which culminated on Oct 17 in the worst rioting France has seen in years.
"The question today is not whether we're going to win" but rather "how much we're going to win", CGT union leader Sophie Binet said at the Paris rally.
The unions are calling for across-the-board wage raises, tax reforms and better learning conditions for young people and have complained about police restrictions on certain protests.
While the marches were largely peaceful, skirmishes between protestors and police broke out in some cities, including Lyon where at least one vehicle was torched and tear gas was fired.
Winegrower Martin Thiberge said he wanted to take part in demonstrations that were drawing together people from across French society.
"We want to make a living from our work, to make a dignified wage," he said at the Lyon protest.
In Marseille, 31-year-old social worker Lea told AFP that she was "fed up with counting every cent."
"This social movement has given us hope," she added.
In Paris, the Eiffel Tower and the Arc de Triomphe, popular among tourists, were closed for the day.
- SCHOOL BLOCKADES -
Dozens of high-schoolers protested in several cities, with the government reporting blockades at 81 out of the country's 3,700 high schools.
A high school student association said classes had been suspended at 1,000 secondary schools.
Around 16 per cent of teachers nationwide were on strike, the education ministry said.
In Paris, police used tear gas to try to prevent students from blocking access to the Helene-Boucher high school in the city's east, an AFP reporter said.
Public and private education unions have called for strike action, as well as unions representing rail workers, public hospitals and postal services.
At the capital's Montparnasse train station, a psychologist who gave her name as Jeanne said her trip had been delayed.
"It's tedious to get up early, wait, and then see your train cancelled, but it's understandable there's a strike," she said.
- POLICE VIOLENCE ALLEGED -

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez announced Wednesday that 70,000 police officers and security forces would be deployed across the country, promising "an extremely firm response" to any "acts of violence" or disorder.
The protests have been largely peaceful, though some disintegrated into clashes with police, who have fired tear gas and water cannon.
An attempted murder investigation has been launched after petrol bombs were thrown at security forces in Paris on Saturday.
The police response has been criticised as heavy-handed and internal police investigations have been launched over allegations of brutality.
Several teenage protesters have been seriously wounded and thousands arrested.
Similar protests have erupted in other European countries in recent weeks.--AFP

9215eda9a087d664: KUALA LUMPUR: Constraints in implementing the Sejahtera People's Housing Programme (PPRS) have prompted the Rural and Regional Development Ministry to reallocate RM200 million from its 2026 allocation to settle outstanding payments for rural road projects.
Deputy Minister Datuk Rubiah Wang said the constraints included land ownership disputes among heirs, a lack of suitable sites and overlapping applicants' names.

She said the reallocation was carried out through a Notice of Change (NOC) from the original PPRS 2026 allocation of RM413 million to prevent the annual allocation from going unspent due to project delays.
However, Rubiah said the adjustment did not mean the ministry was sidelining its welfare agenda and the provision of housing for rural communities.

"Applications for PPRS are indeed very high, but we face various implementation issues on the ground... that is why some projects have had to be postponed and we need to re-examine them, which is why the RM200 million could not be spent.

"That means we can issue a NOC for rural road projects. That is why I said earlier that we are not sacrificing the interests of any particular project," she said when winding up the debate on the Supply Bill 2027 and the Development Expenditure Estimates 2027 at the committee stage for the ministry in the Dewan Rakyat.
For the 2027 Budget, she said the government allocated RM416.2 million for PPRS, which is expected to benefit 12,457 recipients through new housing and home repair projects nationwide.

On rural road projects, Rubiah said implementation had also been affected by a Finance Ministry directive on Sept 10 last year to defer the issuance of Letters of Acceptance (LOA) as a spending control measure.

She said the deferment was for the ministry to stabilise its financial position and settle commitments on earlier projects, but the absence of a fixed timeline from MoF risked causing new project tenders to be cancelled.

"An LOA is valid for only two to three months. If we do not obtain further approval from MoF within six months, the project tender will certainly have to be cancelled and we will need to start a new process," she said.
Under the guidelines for the preparation of the 13th Malaysia Plan, projects that are not tendered or implemented within two years risk being cancelled, she added.
Citing Sabah as an example, she said the issuance of SSTs for 20 rural road projects at the pre-implementation stage were frozen, while 62 projects in the construction phase would proceed.

The Dewan Rakyat then approved the 2027 operating and development expenditure estimates for the ministry, amounting to RM4,850,160,200 under Budget 2027, by a majority vote after 31 MPs debated the estimates.
Before adjourning the sitting, Dewan Rakyat Deputy Speaker Datuk Seri Dr Ramli Mohd Nor took the opportunity to wish all members of the House and Malaysians a Happy Deepavali.

07e85c1b3cdab4c2: TEHRAN: Five oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) and army said in separate statements, according to local media on Thursday.
Since the outbreak of the Iran war in late February, Tehran has severely restricted traffic through the strategic waterway, which normally carries about one-fifth of global oil consumption.

"Last night... a large oil tanker attempting to pass through the illegal passageway south of the Strait of Hormuz suffered a fire after striking a mine and was brought to a halt," the Guards told Fars news agency.

"Early this morning, a violating oil tanker - navigating through an unsafe area east of the Strait of Hormuz - caught fire and came to a halt after striking a naval mine," the army said, according to the official IRNA news agency.

That area is around 500km west of Hormuz, in the centre of the Gulf.
Fars also reported that the IRGC navy's electronic warfare unit had taken control of two LUCAS drones, a US-developed model whose name is short for Low-cost Uncrewed Combat Attack System.
Last month, the US military said it had helped Gulf countries export 1.5 billion barrels of oil via Hormuz since the summer.

5e1bf5f5dd7b2ef8: DUBAI: Iran reported three more tankers had been damaged in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, making clear that shipping would remain in peril as long as the war in the Gulf is unresolved, now that US voters have punished President Donald Trump for waging it.

The electoral rout that cost Trump's Republicans control of Congress has prompted a stark reassessment of the conflict's political cost in Washington, led by Vice President JD Vance, who said in a long social media post on Wednesday that the war was to blame for his party's defeat.

In a mocking reply on Thursday, Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, Vance's opposite number at previous peace talks, accused Vance of letting Trump double down like a "losing gambler" by planning more US strikes.

Oil prices have plunged in recent days as traders wagered that Trump, chastened by voters, may be less likely to restart the strikes he launched alongside Israel as "Operation Epic Fury" in February. Prices bounced back slightly on Thursday but are down more than US$20 a barrel from last week.

ATTACKS ON TANKERS AT RECORD PACE

Iran's Revolutionary Guards, who do not typically acknowledge firing on merchant ships but say the transit route is unsafe without Teheran's consent, said two tankers had struck naval mines and another had caught fire on Thursday.

When asked about Vance's comments on the war on Wednesday, Trump defended the decision to launch it, saying it was important to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, a justification he has repeatedly cited.

A White House adviser told Reuters that some officials and staff inside the White House viewed Vance's post as a foreign policy break from the president and a public recognition of the war's economic consequences.
But two sources told Reuters they believed Trump was still likely to order resumed hostilities.

"He is planning to bomb Iran. Don't listen to what he's saying. He held off because of the midterms. We asked him to hold off until the midterms," said one of the sources. The other said Trump did not ​have anything to lose politically now ⁠that the midterms were over.

Peacemaking efforts have revolved around the future status of the strait, a US blockade on Iranian ports, sanctions on the Islamic Republic and a resumption of negotiations over Teheran's nuclear programme.

444e4a6654475014: KUALA LUMPUR: Shah Alam remains at risk of major flooding unless alternative waterways are built to divert excess rainwater from existing rivers, says former Selangor menteri besar Dr Mohamad Khir Toyo
He said the risk was likely to increase due to rapid development in surrounding areas and Shah Alam's lower elevation compared with neighbouring areas.

Khir Toyo said Shah Alam was situated in a low-lying valley compared with surrounding areas such as Sungai Buloh, Rawang and Petaling Jaya.
"Major floods are likely when heavy rain coincides with high tides.

"This causes water to accumulate and stagnate in low-lying areas such as Shah Alam," he said.

e5187de5927fe656: Trump went to war seeking regime change in Iran. Instead, it was his own grip on Washington that gave way, as voters weary of the war and hit by soaring fuel prices handed Democrats control of Congress.

9aa0c5e4c5d8df0c: Democrats' take over of Congress and growing Republican unease over Israel could trigger the biggest reassessment of United States support for its closest Middle East ally in decades, after an election shaped in part by anger over the Iran war.
Democrats won both the Senate and House in Tuesday's midterms. Many winning candidates were progressives who campaigned against military aid to Israel and the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Israel's campaign in Gaza and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's embrace of President Donald Trump and other Republicans had already strained decades of bipartisan support for Israel.

Democratic control could bring greater scrutiny of military aid and West Bank violence, along with hearings and challenges to Trump nominees, although the president's veto limits the party's ability to force major policy changes.

One successful progressive was Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, the first Muslim elected to the US Senate despite Republican attempts to win over Jewish voters who might have been uncomfortable with his faith and his criticism of Israel.
There were also signs that Republicans might reexamine their party's traditional support for Israel.

Policy towards Israel has emerged as a generational divide in US politics.
Opinion polls show younger voters, including some Republicans, feel the country has been too supportive of Israel and insufficiently supportive of residents of the Palestinian territories.
Congressional sentiment had already been shifting.

In September, 46 of the 47 members of the Senate Democratic caucus voted for a resolution to force Trump's administration to report to Congress on increasing violence against Palestinians by Israeli settlers in the West Bank.
Republicans blocked the measure, but the near-unanimous Democratic vote was a sharp departure from decades of reliable bipartisan backing for Israel.
Democrats will likely focus again on West Bank violence.
"We need to make sure that we apply our laws and international law and our policies uniformly across the board when it comes to the actions of countries.
"There should not be an Israel exception," said Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, who has led attempts to put human rights conditions on Israel aid.

Democrats' power remains limited, however. Trump promised to be "Mr. Veto", and they are unlikely to muster the two-thirds majorities needed to override his vetoes if the president refuses to sign their bills.
Still, there might be enough resistance to sending US tax dollars abroad, and anger over the Iran war, for the "America First" wing of the Republican Party to also push back.

The election result could see "weird bedfellows of left and right come together in condemnation of Israel", said Price Floyd, a former US official and senior adviser with Argyll Strategy, a London-based strategic communications firm.
Majorities also mean Democrats can summon administration officials to public hearings, a rarity under Trump's Republicans.
Opinion polls showed the Iran war was a top election issue. Many Americans blamed higher prices — especially for petrol — on the conflict Trump began in February.

Jonathan Schanzer, executive director of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies think tank, which advocates for a strong US-Israel alliance, said Israel's changing leadership could change the "mood music" of dealings between the two countries.
Netanyahu lost his governing majority in an Oct 27 Israeli election, but denied opponents a clear path to unseat him. Negotiations to form a new government are expected to be protracted.
A new Israeli government, particularly one less closely tied to Republicans, could engage in a more cooperative way with Democrats.
"Nothing is going to change in the US until January when Congress takes their seats and by then, there may be a new Israeli government that would also have an impact on this," said Schanzer.

600826703541818f: The big memory manufacturers continue to print money at the expense of long-suffering buyers, with industry DRAM revenue approaching five times its level a year ago.
Demand for datacenter capacity and AI accelerators drove the 369 percent year-over-year surge in Q3 2026, Counterpoint Research reports.
"Bit shipments rose only about 4 percent this quarter, yet DRAM revenue reached nearly $200 billion, close to 5x a year ago," says Counterpoint senior analyst Jeongku Choi.

"AI has turned memory from a commodity into a valuable scarce resource, and buyers are now competing for supply rather than negotiating on price. With prices still rising, suppliers are on track to set new earnings records again next quarter."

As Reg readers will be well aware by now, the AI infrastructure boom has sent demand for server memory soaring. Manufacturers have prioritized more lucrative products for that market, squeezing supplies for PCs, smartphones, and other devices.

The consequences have been a sharp increase in memory costs, leading to higher prices of products that use it. The average price tag for a laptop or desktop was up by double-digit percentages across Europe this summer, resulting in falling PC shipments as vendors struggled to secure supplies and buyers were put off by the expense.

A similar effect has been seen in the smartphone arena, with shipments down by at least a fifth as rising memory costs squeezed budget models out of the market, leaving vendors to focus on high-end devices instead.

Price increases slowed from the steep rises seen in the first half of the year, Counterpoint says, but average DRAM selling prices still reached $1.90 per gigabit and remained the main driver of revenue growth.

Of the big three memory makers – the DRAMvirate, if you like – Samsung led with a 38 percent share of DRAM revenue. Separately, it forecast company-wide operating profit of about $80 billion for Q3, up from $9 billion a year earlier.

SK hynix posted stronger sequential growth, helping it recover some of the share it lost earlier this year, according to Counterpoint. The firm made a $62.8 billion profit, and predicts that memory shortages will persist until at least 2030.

Micron's DRAM revenue grew more slowly than rivals', but its wider business hardly suffered: fiscal fourth-quarter net profit reached $37.7 billion, exceeding its entire second-quarter revenue of $23.8 billion.
Counterpoint's research director MS Hwang expects to see memory prices remaining high next year.

"[High-bandwidth memory] prices, which lagged commodity DRAM this year, are now catching up. Long-term agreements (LTAs) are supporting prices, and supply will stay tight because major new fabs will not start production until 2028. LTA terms may cause results to differ between suppliers in the short term, but over time they should all follow the same upward trend," he says.
That means more bad news for buyers, but more massive profits for the memory makers. ®

58b7d79929a57f2e: Malaysia faces the threat of cyberattacks, warned Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim.
It is inevitable, driven by Malaysia's 30-year advancement to become Southeast Asia's digital powerhouse.
The boom started in 1996. The first commercial satellite, Measat-1, introduced direct-to-home satellite television.

Soon after, the Multimedia Super Corridor attracted global companies by offering special financial, tax and economic perks. The boom's trifecta was complete: dial-up Internet opened a borderless cyberspace and global e-commerce.
By 2010, the National Information Technology Agenda bridged the digital divide, shifting government counter services online.
In the following decade, high-speed broadband rolled out—digitising enterprises, training Malaysians for digital platforms and opening up social media.
In this decade, the Malaysia Digital Economy Blueprint produced hyper growth, a high-income digital economy and accelerated 5G mobilisation.
Global data centres propelling artificial intelligence are sprouting, including two of the world's biggest in Kempas and Nusantara in Johor, contributing to the gross domestic product through 2038.

According to the Malaysia Digital Economy Corporation, investments under the Malaysia Digital national strategic initiative surged 125 per cent in the second quarter of 2025 to RM29.47 billion from RM13.11 billion in the first quarter.

This could explain the cyberattacks and the price of becoming a digital powerhouse. Since 2016, Malaysia has faced ransomware attacks, breaches of public infrastructure and government networks, and political hacking.

In 2017, 46 million mobile phone subscribers' records were offered for sale. In 2019, 28 million airline customer data records were exposed. In 2022, a domestic airline was hit by a ransomware attack.

In 2023 and 2024, websites were defaced, personal data and intellectual property stolen, and networks breached. In 2024, a ransomware attack hit our mass transit operator, with stolen data published on the dark web.
Last year, the Kuala Lumpur International Airport was hit by a US$10 million ransomware demand while another attack targeted government and private sector organisations.

Protecting the infrastructure powering our ambition is an urgent priority. The first step is raising the National Cyber Threat Level alongside a suite of immediate security measures: 24-hour monitoring, system patching, multi-factor authentication and updated service contingency plans.
The sober reality is that cyberattacks carry consequences well beyond the digital realm. Cybersecurity cannot be left entirely to the government. It requires shared responsibility.

The private sector must also help protect digital infrastructure. Since Malaysia's digital ambitions cannot outpace cyber defence, the real test lies in whether Malaysia can maintain essential services through the next major cyberattack.
