Find all of the previous At the Money episodes here, and in the MiB feed on Apple Podcasts, YouTube, Spotify, and Bloomberg. And find the entire musical playlist of all the songs I have used on At the Money on Spotify
TRANSCRIPT:
Bloomberg · Barry Ritholtz with Brian Portnoy, CEO of Shaping Wealth · Transcript

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Most investment authors tell you what to do with your money, but they never reveal what they do with their own money. That bothered Brian Portnoy. He spent more than 20 years in the mutual fund and hedge fund industries. He holds a PhD from the University of Chicago, and he is the CEO of Shaping Wealth. His 2018 book, The Geometry of Wealth, was really a fascinating exploration of behavioral finance and emotional intelligence. He has co-edited two editions of How I Invest My Money with my partner Josh Brown—full disclosure, Josh is at Ritholtz Wealth Management. So let’s talk a little bit about both of these books. They’re really very different from the usual investment tomes. Tell me a little bit about their genesis.

BRIAN PORTNOY: Thanks, Barry. Appreciate it. The genesis is a fun little story. It was 2019, and Josh, who you know and I know is a very sharp and good writer, published a blog with the title “How I Invest My Money,” and he made the simple observation that in all the years that he’s been in the market, no one’s really ever asked him for investment advice or financial planning advice. So he decided to write a blog that walked through how he builds his portfolio, venture investments in friends’ companies, a variety of things. And it got great feedback. It was very well done. I read it, I texted him, I said, “This was great, and hey, what do you think about getting a bunch of our friends together to write similar short blogs or chapters, and we could put it together as a volume?” And he loved the idea. I called our friend Craig Pierce at Harriman House and said, “Craig, what do you think?” I’ll say, from me texting Josh to us having a book contract was about 72 hours. Harriman House was very into it. Josh and I proceeded to build a volume of 25 contributors, and that volume was published in 2020 and really received wonderful reviews. And as you indicated, we’ve followed up with a second volume very recently.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So the really interesting thing about this is, with some people who are free to share their advice, the question comes up: Hey, might they be a little reluctant to open the kimono about how they run their own books, their own portfolios, their own household finances? Did you get any pushback from people who were a little reluctant to drop their professional personas and speak honestly about what they do with their own money?
BRIAN PORTNOY: The short answer is no. For the first volume, 25 phone calls, 25 chapters.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: Really?
BRIAN PORTNOY: Yeah, 25 for 25.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: That’s amazing. Second one, no hesitation? Nobody tapped out? Nobody said, “Not for me”?

BRIAN PORTNOY: Second volume, 25 for 25. But your word—hesitation. So here’s the thing, and a word that has surfaced with the publishing of these two volumes that I think is so important to being successful financially, which is permission. Effectively, we gave permission to people. They happen to be financial experts, financial advisors, portfolio managers, economists, and the like. But we gave permission to, quote unquote, go there—talk about how you invest your money. Because think about an equity fund manager. Well, they might run a large-cap equity sleeve and be very good at that, but when they think about running their money, well, they’re going to have lots of equities, lots of bonds, they’re going to have real estate, they’re going to be doing a lot of different things with their money beyond the portfolio. Charitable giving and insuring and risk management, on and on. And so the stories ended up being this unbelievable kaleidoscope of different journeys. And Barry, it’s the part that I’m proudest of in this ongoing project. Now 50 chapters, 50 completely distinct life stories from people who all know, quote unquote, the right answer. But then when invited to—and again, given their permission—to really talk about how they invest, how they allocate to the things that are important to them, they went in their own direction and expressed it in a very unique way.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: So I’m really curious about both the first 25 people in the first book and the second 25 people—or I should say the other 24 people, because I’m one of them in the second book.
BRIAN PORTNOY: Yep.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: How did you put that list together? Did you just go through the contacts on your phone, or was there a “Hey, let’s have a few of these and a few of those”? What did that look like?

BRIAN PORTNOY: It was important for me to have a diverse set of voices. One of the outcomes that I want from this ongoing project is for readers—just regular folks, friends and neighbors—to pick up the volume. You’ve now got 50 four-page chapters, very easy bite-size insights. I want people to find voices that resonate with them. And so it was important for me that we have people further along in their career, we have people who are relatively young, we have men, we have women, we have people of color. We’ve just got sort of a differentiated set of perspectives that tie into individual journeys, and those are what they are. The feedback that we’ve gotten from so many readers is exactly that: One, I was able to find some voices that really synced with my life experience, and then secondly, I read chapters from other contributors and I would’ve never thought about that particular perspective or journey. So I think it was important in both volumes to have a mix of people so that everyone can appreciate the diversity of experiences that we have with our money stories.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: Did contributors get a brief—“Hey, we want you to talk about this or that”—or was it just a blank page without any structure and, “Hey, we want a thousand words. Knock yourself out”?

BRIAN PORTNOY: Completely blank page. There was a one-line instruction: Answer the question, how do you invest your money? You contributed, you saw that firsthand. In the second volume, people could look back and see what folks did in the first volume. But with the first volume, this being just a total greenfield experiment, what was really neat was to see that we gave that simple instruction and people tended not to answer the question “how I invest my money.” They leaned into why I invest my money, because we got all these wonderful stories about families and priorities and hopes and dreams and fears. So it really isn’t sort of a bullet-point list of, “Hey, I have a 75% allocation to equity and a 20% allocation to bonds and 5% allocation to real estate.” That’s not the way these turned out. Some people went into more detail on their specific investments, but without asking, what the contributors did across all 50 chapters was basically say: This is my life. This is what’s important to me, and this is how I allocate my capital. I mean, you in particular, Barry, were one of a handful of people in the two volumes who pointed out that when we’re talking about money, we’re actually talking about our capital—our financial capital, our temporal capital, our social capital, our human capital. And we’re all making decisions about what those are and how we want to invest them in order to live the life that we want.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: I’m curious about the use of proceeds. I should have asked you this earlier, but let’s talk about the royalties on this book. This isn’t just a money grab for the authors. Tell us a little bit about that.

BRIAN PORTNOY: Anyone who publishes a book outside of someone like our friend Morgan Housel knows there’s not a lot of money in this. There really isn’t. So no, this was a labor of love. Everybody contributed their chapters without any expectation of compensation. And as I said to several of the contributors to the two volumes, if you want one twenty-fifth of the proceeds, I’m happy to send that to you. Or I could just send you a Starbucks gift card so that you can get maybe a large coffee.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So I’m curious as to the biggest surprises in each edition. What chapters kind of leapt out at you and said, “Hey, I’ve never really thought about this aspect of money and investing quite this way before”?

BRIAN PORTNOY: It’s a good question, and I think back—volume one was published six years ago, so I’ll have to rack my brain a little bit. It was really the stories that people surfaced, and how well they were able to articulate things in their lives that brought them joy, that were important to them. So in the first volume, a couple or three people. I mean, Bob Seawright wrote a beautiful chapter about a cottage, a vacation home that his family has had for a couple of generations. And his chapter on how I invest my money was really about how do they maintain that house as a place where grandparents, parents, and grandkids can come together and enjoy life. At the same time, Dasarte Yarnway in volume one wrote a beautiful chapter—it was sort of an immigrant’s tale about how his family came from Africa, built a life in America, and how that influenced the way Dasarte thinks about his portfolio and supporting his family and community. Leighann Miko, writing about growing up in pretty intense scarcity and how that impacted her perspective on becoming a financial advisor who could help people really come along. So volume one—you asked about surprising. I wouldn’t say that I was terribly surprised. I thought I knew most of these people reasonably well. It was a delight to read their life story and learn something new about them. And the same experience carried over to volume two. Heather Robertson Fortner wrote a very personal tale about some intense childhood struggles she had that established and changed her lens on money. Samantha Russell, who many in the industry know well—tragically, at a very young age, she lost her husband to cancer and has three small children, and asked some very profound questions about what does any of this matter? Basically, like, how do I invest my money? Like, who gives a flip? I’ve had this tragedy and it has made it so clear what’s truly important. And so the money questions, which are real—because you need the portfolio, you need the insurance, you need to have the estate plan, and thankfully they had that in place before her husband passed—all of that is in this broader context of navigating life’s ups and downs, uncertainties, happiness, tragedy, and so forth. The surprise with someone’s financial strategy, not so much. The surprise is usually delightful in terms of, wow, I didn’t know that about this person—on almost every page.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Huh, really interesting. So the underlying thesis is, hey, people always tell you what to do, but they don’t tell you what they do. I’m curious: Where were the biggest gaps between the typical investment recommendations and the sort of things people either actually do or think about and talk about as part of their approach to investing?

BRIAN PORTNOY: I think across all 50 chapters, you see a pretty subjective approach to risk. We know technically that risk can be measured and managed in some quantitative ways that tell us whether or not we’re taking too much, too little, or the right amount of risk. I think what we saw across many of the chapters were narratives about how attitudes toward risk, which tended to come from childhood and adolescent experiences, then later influenced an approach to managing the family finances. A couple of specific examples. Mortgages, I think—and we could talk about whether there’s a sample bias in who came along for this journey. But on the mortgage front, there are a number of people who indicated that they paid off their mortgage early. You can run the math and you could say, well, if I don’t pay off my mortgage early and I take that extra cash flow and I invest it in the market, there’s probably going to be—depending on your rate—a delta between the rate of return in the market and your mortgage rate, and hopefully that’s a positive delta. And so it’s, quote unquote, rational to not pay off your mortgage—forget about it. A number of people, including me, have paid off their mortgage at one point or another because it just feels good to know that, leaving aside taxes, you own your home and you’re safe and you’re secure. The number one question with our money lives, with financial planning across the board, is simply: Am I going to be okay? You saw lots of these financial experts in their own way answer the question, am I going to be okay? Paying off the mortgage is one thing. Establishing that safety, holding a lot of cash—another theme that came up multiple times across both volumes. There’s a, quote unquote, optimal level of cash that you want to have in your portfolio relative to the risk you’re taking, relative to your monthly expenses, and whether you set aside six months of living expenses, whatever rule you choose. Lo and behold, we saw a number of people hold what the theory would say is too much cash. But in the same vein as paying off mortgages early, there’s a certain element of safety that comes through that, and you forsake maybe higher long-term returns for that feeling of safety now.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: We’ve all had this conversation with people, and I believe the question that we often ask is wrong. It’s not, which is mathematically the optimum solution. The question is, for you and your personality and your risk tolerance and your just sense of wellbeing, are you willing to do what is suboptimal mathematically for something that is going to be—I don’t want to say optimal, but much better psychologically, much better in terms of your comfort level? A lot of—I don’t want to say left-brain people, but a lot of the math people. And just as an aside, my CFO, Bill Sweet, and I have this ongoing discussion about, do you take the cash back on your credit card or do you take the points? And Bill, who is a CFO, says, “Well, of course you take the cash back.” And me, who has been married for nearly 35 years, says, “No, I want the points,” because $43.72 dropping into my checking account will kind of sneak by unnoticed. But when I want to buy that really stupid cappuccino maker for two grand and my wife is going to make me sleep in the backyard—“Honey, I’m getting it with points.” “Oh, go ahead then.” So sometimes the optimal mathematical solution may not be the optimal human solution.

BRIAN PORTNOY: So Daniel Crosby, who is a good friend and an expert in behavioral finance, wrote exactly about this and used the line that there’s a difference between spreadsheet optimal and behaviorally optimal. So in a sense, How I Invest My Money, both volumes one and two, are sort of masterclasses in applied behavioral finance, because we’re asking the experts to reflect on which version of optimal are you going to choose. And across the board, it was the behaviorally optimal path that they took. We know that the best financial plan is the plan that you can stick with. And so if you build the perfect plan according to modern portfolio theory, but it introduces behavioral risks that the client can’t manage, well, then you don’t have a good portfolio. So unfortunately for the ultra-left-brain folks among us, it’s life. It’s a mess. But this is what we do. This is the good stuff.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Wes Gray of Alpha Architect wrote a white paper a couple of years ago where the highest-returning combination of factors was something like deep value and momentum, but it was so volatile and the drawdowns were so fierce that he titled the paper “Even God Would Get Fired as an Active Manager.” Just to give you an idea.
BRIAN PORTNOY: I love that piece.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: The difference between mathematically and behaviorally optimum. Second to last question: Any conflicting approaches? Are there, throughout the books, different chapters that sort of lie in opposition to each other? Or are they really more, listen, we kind of forget personal finance is personal, and what’s right for one person may not be right for another?

BRIAN PORTNOY: Tim Maurer has that great line that personal finance is more personal than finance. So based on risk tolerances or approach to risk, mapping it up to goals, short-term and long-term, you see a pretty wide range of people who have more aggressive portfolios versus more conservative portfolios. The key is to understand the why. So what is it about who you are now and what you want to achieve, but also your experiences that got you here, that led you to have a portfolio that’s more balanced between stocks and bonds versus one that’s entirely in equities, where you’re okay with taking what’s likely to be more volatility in the hopes that that portfolio returns more over time? So I’d say that there are disagreements across the chapters if you put them in the same room in terms of how to invest. But the point is that all of these folks, all 50 of them, are saying, well, this is the way I invest, and it’s not in conflict with how I might manage client assets. It’s just that what I do for them isn’t perfectly mapping to my life and my constraints—taking care of kids, supporting parents as they age, things you want to do in the community. Imagine the full range of choices that we have. Even if you’re a seasoned portfolio manager with an outstanding track record or a financial advisor who’s been taking care of families for the last 20 or 30 years, your life circumstances are yours. Everybody is quite unique. So that’s what makes these chapters so fun and colorful. You could just find different smart people doing it differently.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: And last question: Did editing the book change how you invest your own money, or what you wanted to accomplish with that money?

BRIAN PORTNOY: No. No, because I think good financial planning starts by looking in the mirror. And that’s something that I’ve done a lot. I think I’ve been reasonably thoughtful about who I am and my money journey. I write about this and do this for a living. I have what I think is a healthy, ongoing dialogue with my wife about this. Increasingly we’re folding our adult children into more mature conversations about finances and legacy and things like that. So I was delighted to see the range of perspectives, the way folks wrote about answering, well, how much is enough? What risks should I take? How do I navigate this complex relationship? I learned a lot, but in terms of the way that we’ve managed our own financial assets and my philosophy, which is really based around simplicity, diversification, and compounding—I would say that those have been some anchor principles for me for a very long time. And those did not change based on editing these chapters.
5c5885d9a73a4b1e: JAKARTA: Several Indonesian political parties are considering a parliamentary inquiry into the validity of Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka's diploma as a rift intensifies between President Prabowo Subianto and his predecessor Joko Widodo, Gibran's father.

The proposal emerged after the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court ruled that Gibran's foreign senior high school credentials did not meet domestic legal requirements for vice-presidential candidates, and had been improperly accepted by election officials.

It also followed the arrest of Prabowo's former chief of staff, Listyo Sigit Prabowo, in a wiretapping scandal that the government said could amount to treason. Listyo, also a former national police chief, was known as a Widodo loyalist.
Seven of the eight parties in parliament have joined Prabowo's coalition, giving him a majority. Neither Jokowi nor Gibran has a party represented in parliament.
Three parties within Prabowo's camp and one outside the coalition said they were currently considering three legislative courses of action, officials said.
Under the Constitution, lawmakers can seek an explanation from the government, launch an inquiry or investigation, or formally express their position on alleged legal or constitutional violations.
Each option can be an initial step towards impeachment proceedings. None of the parties involved mentioned the prospect of impeachment.
"We are currently reviewing these options and also communicating with other political parties," said Muhammad Kholid, a senior official of the Prosperous Justice Party.
Most parties have reached a consensus that the two court rulings must be followed up by the parliament, he told Reuters.
Another party within Prabowo's camp, the National Awakening Party, is "seriously" considering the three options, said party official Muhammad Khozin in a statement.

Golkar Party lawmaker Ahmad Doli Kurnia said formally expressing their position would be the most relevant response to the courts' rulings, local media reported. Golkar, another party in Prabowo's coalition, has the second largest number of seats in parliament.
The vice president's office did not respond to a request for comment.

The only party outside Prabowo's coalition, Indonesian Democratic Party of Struggle, said recent public dissatisfaction stemming from Gibran's diploma, as well as the wiretapping cases, has prompted lawmakers to take action.
"There's increasingly intensive dialogue in the parliament to invoke their constitutional rights especially after the wiretapping," said the party's top official, Hasto Kristiyanto.--REUTERS

<!--kg-card-end: html--> There's a BlazeTV YouTube video whose thumbnail shows the presenter with his arms around Anakin Skywalker and a gender-flipped Draco Malfoy called Malfoid. “Total Chud Victory?” It says. The video's title: “Young Right is Reclaiming Culture and Liberals Are Mad About it.”

BlazeTV posted the video on November 2, the day before Democrats swept the midterms and started a political realignment in America so overwhelming that Republicans lost control of all the most powerful state positions in Texas.

The video is a profound misreading of the political and cultural moment. It reminded me of stories of the Bolsheviks seizing the Winter Palace to discover tarot card playing courtiers who had no idea a revolution was happening in the streets.

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> The American version was watching defense contractor Palmer Lucky dress up like Harry Potter on Halloween while standing next to his Malfoid wife. And it was Elon Musk — who spent roughly half a billion on the election only to see his chosen candidates fail — posting an AI generated picture of Anakin Skywalker sitting at the head of a happy fascist Star Wars family two days before the midterms.
This is what they stole from us pic.twitter.com/q1GnpjF394
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 1, 2026

The online right has dominated American culture for a decade, or at least has dominated political narratives picked up by the mainstream media. Its memes and conspiracies drove news cycles. At first, the right’s memes filtered from random people on obscure Discord channels to Reddit’s r/the_donald or 4chan to Trump’s Twitter feed. More recently they’ve come from AI slop farms, from Musk, or from the administration itself. Powered by a well-funded media and podcast ecosystem, Fox News (and a propensity for shamelessness) its comedians, podcasters, and pundits became powerful celebrities and influencers, at least within Elon Musk’s X.

This insular, often inscrutable world has given us Ben Shapiro, Nick Fuentes, Gamergate influencers, the streamer Asmongold, and a revolving door of characters who have shuffled interchangeably between Twitterverse celebritydom and actual government; Kash Patel, DataRepublican, Laura Loomer, Pete Hegseth, RFK Jr., Dan Bongino, the list goes on.

It has been said many times that “Twitter is not real life,” and that posting too much anywhere will rot your brain. Never has that been more apparent than now: Much of Trumpworld spent the week before an election in which they would get utterly trounced using AI to generate barely legible Anakin and Malfoid memes for an inconsequential ingroup on the social media platform run by the biggest loser on the planet.

“It certainly seems like it has had its high water mark and that reality has FINALLY caught up with the Republican Party,” Michael Senters, a research assistant at the Anti-Defamation League who studies online and gaming culture, told 404 Media.

In 2016, 4chan posters talked about “meme magic” — the pseudo-ironic belief that pictures on the internet could manifest great change in reality. According to legend, Trump strategist Steve Bannon was running a World of Warcraft gold farm when he realized the angry gamers could be harnessed into a powerful reactionary political force. Bannon and others would successfully parlay Gamergate into an endless culture war that’s dominated online life in the Trump era.

During the midterm livestream of Bannon’s War Room podcast, his guest read exit polls that suggested the right-wing had lost young men — a group long thought to be its strongest soldiers. The split between the parties was even, the guest explained. “That can’t be right,” Bannon whispered, signalling he’d lost touch with the constituency he’d harnessed on behalf of Trump ten years ago. As the election results began coming in, right-wing podcasters, livestreamers, and newscasters across the internet went through at least a few of the stages of grief. First they struggled to understand what was happening, suggesting the votes must be wrong. Eventually, many of them ragequit.

"Okay, I'm going to be honest. I'm absolutely rage quitting. I'm so frustrated. I am so unbelievably frustrated. I'm so mad. I think Trump didn't do 50 different things he should have done. I think he should have gone a thousand times harder. I think that he wasted his time selling trinkets and nonsense,” Asmongold said as the returns came in. He lives in Texas where Democrats swept in a shock victory.

“I wish that there were more people who thought like me that weren’t sorry about it. But you know what? There’s not. So it’s just me. And that’s fine. It’s fine. It’s OK,” he said, his voice catching in his throat.

Asmongold (@Asmongold) realizing in real time that he's a total fucking moron who got duped by the most cartoonishly obvious con-man of all time and ragequitting his election night coverage pic.twitter.com/XgtnqNjAaf
— kilo (@kilotonics) November 4, 2026

Many right-wing personalities went into Tuesday somehow expecting to win despite a disastrous war, a disastrous economy, disastrous polls, and a doddering president whose closing argument seemed to be more about his ballrooms, golf courses, and the Reflecting Pool than anything else. Since Trump was re-elected, these same people have called everyone else out of touch, convinced by their X algorithm and prediction markets that no blue wave would materialize. The media has similarly spent many thousands of words suggesting that Bluesky is an out-of-touch leftist echo chamber while mostly failing to suggest anything of the sort about the AI-pilled Silicon Valley executives, bots, and racists shitposting on X. Tuesday’s election wipeout highlights how detached from reality the Malfoid/Anakin-shipping, X-brained billionaires and their acolytes have actually become.

“Blueskywave. Those of us on here, across the board, were out of touch. I see no other conclusion,” Joe Weisenthal of Bloomberg's Odd Lots podcast (who is a serious, good journalist), said in a post on X after the election amidst a sea of Anakins tonguing Malfoids.
"I see through the lies of the Democrats."
VOTE STRAIGHT TICKET REPUBLICAN pic.twitter.com/i1HjdHdAn7
— Utah College Republicans (@UtahCollegeReps) November 1, 2026

The meme game and general demeanor of Trump and his followers has grown wildly tiresome in his thus far-disastrous second term. Under the guidance of White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, official government accounts have posted racist Halo memes, used AI to put a studio Ghibli face on anti-immigrant propaganda, and fully embraced Malfoid and Darth Vader as cultural heroes. The base on X loved this stuff. No one else did.

As our friend Gita Jackson over at Aftermath wisely put it immediately before the election, "The idea that they can meme magic their way into a red sweep by posting about Anakin Skywalker a lot is pure desperation [...] Their values have been rejected by popular culture at large, and they are now resigned to exist in the margins.”

Senters said the midterms showed the hard limits of memes as a political tool. “The power that memes have has always been, in my opinion, the power to help define linguistic and community lines in the amorphous space of the Internet. You create a community when you ‘get the joke’ behind a meme but memes generally don't persuade,” he said. “I'll be curious to see if the government accounts will continue to post these far-right cultural memes in the wake of the defeat or if they'll change their tune at all. Like do they double down on the meme posting to try to rally their base? Because it very clearly had ZERO appeal to anyone outside their base.”

Yet the right-wing has spent the last ten years acting as if their memes had moved the country politically. “They deluded themselves into believing that memes carry persuasive power and that their bubble on X represented material reality in a meaningful way when that was no way close to the truth,” he said. “They saw how many ‘numbers’ the Malfoid and Anakin memes did on X and convinced themselves that this was a real cultural awakening moment and that the volk were on their side.”
It cannot be overstated how culturally significant Anakin poasting is. I dont think you could engineer a better anti-progressive memetic virus in lab if you tried.
— Max (@minordissent) October 31, 2026

Alyssa Mercante, an internet culture reporter who is writing a book about politics and video games called Rage Game, agreed. “I think what it's really showing is that when you start to get a little bit too deep in the weeds of this hyper online culture war stuff, it cannot escape the internet,” Mercante told 404 Media. “It is not working anymore. The material reality of America is just not good enough.” Gas prices are up. Everything is more expensive. And ICE has killed Americans in the streets.

“This conspiratorial mindset is wrecker mentality. It is just destructive for the sake of destruction. There is no goal beyond pulling away any sort of legitimacy from the media or from democracy,” Mercante said. “When you get so deep in the weeds of this anti-establishment conspiratorial thought process, you just can't make anything or do anything of value. You're just upending tables and pointing at them and laughing.”

Democrats crushed Republicans who leaned into the online culture war during the midterms. Bo French — an overt racist who ran for railroad commissioner in Texas — sent text messages to voters that depicted himself as Master Chief from Halo. His opponent beat him by more than a million votes.

In Nevada, Halo composer Martin O’Donnell ran as a Republican for a House seat and lost to incumbent Susie Lee. O’Donnell announced his campaign on Discord and leaned hard into an extremely online gamer identity. “He’s like, ‘I wrote the Halo music and I’m voting for Trump and you should too.’ He did a Halo LAN party campaign fundraiser. The imagery was him as Master Chief,” Mercante said. “This dude is like: ‘My personality is gamers, gamers are not woke and they're resisting this [...] and Trump is the person that is going to help us resist,’ and he's polling like absolute dog water.”

It’s been 12 years since Gamergate set the tempo for online culture wars and a decade since Trump won in 2016. In 2026, Star Wars, Halo, Harry Potter feel dated in a way they didn’t back then. “What 22-year-old kid is going to be like ‘they took Halo from me.’ They don’t know Halo to have it taken away from them,” Mercante said.

She stressed that so much right wing online culture is about distraction — she likened it to jingling keys to capture the attention of a baby. “If the economy is the number one issue for both Democrats and Republicans going into the midterms, no amount of Malfoid scissoring Anakin Skywalker is going to change that need for people to be in a better financial position,” Mercante said. “The tech oligarchs pushed this stuff straight into our eyes for two years straight unfettered [...] And I wake up and gas is this expensive? I don’t care if you take a Taylor Swift song and make JD Vance walk out to it.”

“[They] really thought that this would just last forever,” she added. “When you build up a meme presidency, eventually the cards just collapse underneath you, and there's just nothing to show for it.”

Though this midterm signals a move away from Gamergate-style culture war politics, both Senters and Mercante cautioned that this type of rhetoric is still dangerous, and can still be destructive. “They’re still very good at doing propaganda on the internet — they wrote the book in many cases,” Mercante said.

189779f0923d5df3: For months I’ve been speaking to an AI fraud kingpin. You might remember in 2024 we revealed the existence of OnlyFake, an underground site that let anyone generate realistic photos of fake IDs using ‘neural networks’. The creator of that site went by the handle John Wick. A while later, the creator was arrested.

Turns out there was a lot more to that story. Yuriy Nazarenko, the creator of OnlyFake, told me his side of it. How when I published my initial article he panicked, and destroyed his laptop and emails and got a new phone, paranoid that authorities were about to bust down his door. How the pressure of a growing fraud empire pushed him to drugs. And how North Korean fake IT workers used his site. Read below for his story.
The Confessions of an AI Fraud Kingpin

A few years ago, Yuriy Nazarenko sat at a desk in his grandfather’s apartment in Ukraine and, on a diet of cigarettes, Lay’s chips, and beer, painstakingly made digital copies of fake identity documents. One of his four computer screens had the messaging app Telegram open. Another displayed a scan of a passport in Photoshop filling the entire monitor.

Pixel by pixel, with rap music blaring, Nazarenko edited each part of the passport. That included the MRZ codes, the block of text printed at the bottom of identity documents; the photographs to superimpose someone else’s face into the document; and the overall dimensions and quirks of each different type of passport. Nazarenko would sometimes sit for more than 12 hours at his computer, obsessively tinkering away, with a single, high-quality fake identity document taking up to a week of work.

When someone thinks of fake IDs, maybe they imagine a spotty underage teen buying a physical counterfeit drivers’ license so they can score some beer. But in the global criminal underworld, digital copies or scans of IDs are like a skeleton key. A convincing scan of an ID or utility bill, loaded with a bogus name or someone else’s identity, can unlock the ability to make bank accounts, bypass checks on cryptocurrency exchanges to buy or sell more Bitcoin, or rent a safehouse, all while keeping the criminal’s real identity hidden. The digitally altered IDs need to fool both human reviewers and automated systems that scan them for inconsistencies. Making fake IDs requires exquisite attention to detail.

All of that manual labor doesn’t really scale, Nazarenko thought to himself as he meticulously edited passport after passport. He went on to make templates of fake identity documents that sped up the process, but it was still slow.

After many of these quiet nights, he had an idea. He built a website to automate the process that autopopulated a fake ID with the personal data a customer wanted, rather than having him do it by hand. Then, when generative AI became mainstream a short while later, he incorporated that too.
“That gradually became OnlyFake,” Nazarenko told me.

OnlyFake, the underground website Nazarenko made, landed like a bomb in the fraud world. It allowed anyone to generate not only convincing scans of drivers’ licenses or passports, but also realistic looking photos of those fake identity documents laying on a sofa, carpet, or desk, as if someone had taken the ID out of their wallet and snapped a picture of it on their phone. Needed a convincing looking photo of a California drivers’ license to open a cryptocurrency account in someone else’s name? Or a British passport to incorporate a company overseas? Or a Social Security card? No problem. The results were photos of identity documents that didn’t really exist, of people who may not be real, but yet could trick the sorts of people and companies that verify documents.

With OnlyFake, you didn’t have to be a master forger like Nazarenko to make fake documents. Now, anyone could churn out fake IDs at scale, sometimes even hundreds or thousands at a time. OnlyFake threatened the entire idea of know-your-customer, or KYC, where financial institutions take steps to know who exactly are using its services. When anyone can make a photo of a fake ID for just a few dollars in Bitcoin, is anyone really who they say they are?

Nazarenko didn’t know it then, hunched over his desk, but OnlyFake would soon become so influential that it would spawn copy cats, and the FBI would eventually arrest Nazarenko and shut down some of its competitors. The Department of Justice said in an announcement about Nazarenko’s guilty plea that OnlyFake made more than a million dollars selling fake IDs for just $15 a pop.

Now for the first time, Nazarenko, 28, free after a year in prison and living in Asia, is telling his story: how North Korean fake IT workers used his creation, how he ended up in ICE detention for months after serving his sentence in the U.S., and how OnlyFake unleashed a new age of AI-powered fraud. Nazarenko said he wanted to talk to me because I was the first journalist to reveal that OnlyFake existed. This article is based on interviews with Nazarenko and his lawyer; court records; and my own reporting in the online world of fraud that OnlyFake inhabited.

“OnlyFake was the first time I saw how quickly a small internet project could turn into something global. Unfortunately, it also taught me, in a very painful way, what can happen when the scale of something grows faster than your understanding of its consequences,” Nazarenko told me.

Growing up, Nazarenko’s parents questioned whether Nazarenko would ever find a job. His father worked for the Security Service of Ukraine. Raised in a suburb outside of Odesa, Nazarenko jumped between a few different gigs. He worked as a cook, a waiter, at a supermarket, and as a cameraman at a local Ukrainian TV station.

d7f70096c08caee9: PETALING JAYA: Bersatu's Pengkalan Batu candidate Norhizam Hassan Baktee has given those who circulated an old video, which showed him in an altercation with local authority officers, 24 hours to issue a public apology and set the record straight.

053bb3fdbc0be11b: BANGKOK: A giant rodent weighing around 30 kilogrammes roamed what is now southern Thailand 33 to 35 million years ago, scientists said, after identifying a previously unknown species from two fossilised teeth.
The ancient animal, which one geologist on the team called a "giant rat", was among the largest known from the Paleogene period, offering new clues about how early rodents evolved to enormous sizes.
The findings, published Wednesday in the journal Scientific Reports, were based on a molar and an incisor discovered in 2004 at a coal mine in southern Krabi province.
Pannipa Tian, a geologist with Thailand's Department of Mineral Resources who found the incisor, said she initially misidentified the fossil because of its "unusually large size."
"At first, I thought it was a bone. I showed it to my supervisor, who told me it was a giant rat's tooth," Pannipa, 51, told AFP on Thursday.
The cream-coloured fossil stood out against the dark coal deposits, while another expedition member found the dark-coloured molar the same day.
The Krabi basin has previously yielded fossils of ancient primates, carnivores and hoofed mammals.
But at the time of the discovery, the team lacked sufficient evidence and technology to identify the species.
More than two decades later, researchers from Thailand, France and Canada were able to do so through detailed analysis of the teeth.
The animal weighed around 30 kilogrammes – an estimated half as much as a large capybara, the world's largest living rodent, they said.
Unlike the South American capybara, however, the prehistoric rodent belonged to the now-extinct Ischyromyidae family, one of the earliest major groups of rodents.
"It tells a lot about the diversity of life in the past," Pannipa said, suggesting that ancient rodents may have evolved in what is now Thailand before spreading to other parts of the world.
But with only two teeth recovered, the animal's appearance, diet and behaviour remain unknown.
The species was named Yakamys sirindhornae in honour of Thailand's Princess Sirindhorn, a supporter of scientific and palaeontological research.--AFP
32161c6b507cff6c: MELAKA: The Melaka government intends to market its 'Kampung Digital' (Digital Village) model across the Asean region once the rural digitalisation initiative has been fully streamlined and upgraded.

Caretaker Melaka Chief Minister Datuk Seri Ab Rauf Yusoh said the model holds strong potential to be introduced to neighbouring countries as an innovative framework for residential address management and public service delivery.
He stressed, however, that the platform must undergo continuous refinement before it can be scaled up internationally.

"It must certainly be updated and enhanced to a standard where it can be marketed not only domestically, but also at the Asean level. We could potentially market it to Indonesia, Cambodia, Thailand, and Vietnam," he said.
He said this during a recording session of the Podcast Utama Edisi Khas Buletin TV3 for the 16th Melaka State Election.

Ab Rauf said 'Kampung Digital' was conceived to overcome structural flaws in traditional rural addressing, where hundreds of residents often shared a single generic postal address, complicating postal deliveries and emergency responses.
He said that the introduction of specific house numbers and QR codes allows residential properties to be pinpointed with pinpoint accuracy, assisting emergency rescue units and local authorities.
He noted that public sector technological adoption must accelerate so that government delivery mechanisms keep pace with commercial digital services.
"Digital development must stay aligned with the actual needs of the community.

"It is rather embarrassing that after nearly 70 years of nationhood, deliveries from Shopee, Lazada, McDonald's, and Grab can reach our doorsteps without fail, yet government letters cannot," he said.

Ab Rauf added that the digital addressing initiative has also been extended to cemetery management via the 'Kubur Digital' initiative, enabling heirs and family members to locate ancestral gravesites easily.

Furthermore, he said the state has introduced dedicated domain email accounts for every household registered under Kampung Digital, which will help streamline communications between schools and parents.
"Under my administration, the Melaka state government is offering a state domain by assigning an email address to every household under Kampung Digital.

"With these email addresses, the platform will interface with the Education Department, which I currently oversee, enabling teachers to connect directly with parents via email—for example, alerting them if a child has missed school for three consecutive days," he said.
5d62d26cdf13c437: KUALA LUMPUR: Kementerian Kewangan akan menentukan sama ada projek pembangunan luar bandar yang ditangguhkan pengeluaran surat setuju terimanya (SST) boleh diteruskan atau sebaliknya, kata Timbalan Menteri Kemajuan Desa dan Wilayah Rubiah Wang.

Beliau berkata, kementeriannya mematuhi keputusan Kementerian Kewangan untuk menangguhkan semua SST yang belum dikeluarkan, termasuk yang sedang menunggu giliran pengeluaran serta projek yang sudah sedia untuk ditender.
"Keputusan Kementerian Kewangan ini tidak ada garis masa. Tidak ada garis masa ... SST hanya sah untuk dua, tiga bulan sahaja," katanya di Dewan Rakyat.
"Maksudnya dalam tempoh enam bulan, kalaulah kita tidak mendapat 'endorsement' lanjut daripada Kementerian Kewangan, sudah pasti projek itu terpaksa dibatalkan dan kita mulakan dengan proses baharu."

Rubiah berkata demikian sebagai respons terhadap Chong Zhemin (PH-Kampar), yang meminta pengesahan sama ada benar tiada projek pembangunan luar bandar di Sabah yang dibatalkan, sebaliknya hanya ditangguhkan, susulan penggantungan pengeluaran SST tersebut.

Beliau menjelaskan, langkah Kementerian Kewangan menangguhkan SST itu bertujuan menstabilkan kedudukan kewangan Kementerian Kemajuan Desa dan Wilayah (KKDW), khususnya membabitkan peruntukan kementerian.
"Kita menjangkakan perkara ini malah akan terjadi dalam dua, tiga tahun, kalau tidak diambil tindakan segera," kata Rubiah.

"Jadi, sekiranya kita ambil kira satu lagi garis panduan yang digunakan dalam RMK13 (Rancangan Malaysia ke-13), penyediaan projek yang tidak dapat ditender atau tidak dilaksanakan dalam tempoh dua tahun, potensi projek itu dibatalkan adalah tinggi."

Bulan lepas, Timbalan Perdana Menteri Zahid Hamidi memberitahu Dewan Rakyat, beberapa projek di Sabah dan Sarawak yang diluluskan bagi tahun ini ditangguhkan atas arahan ketua setiausaha KKDW, walaupun peruntukan mengenainya sudah disediakan.
Zahid yang juga menteri kemajuan desa dan wilayah berkata, SST yang telah diserahkan kepada kontraktor sebelum ini turut dibatalkan.

Bagaimanapun, Menteri Kewangan II Amir Hamzah Azizan menegaskan kerajaan hanya menangguhkan pengeluaran SST baharu sehingga bayaran tertunggak kepada kontraktor dilunaskan, selain memaklumkan bahawa tiada sebarang surat yang telah dikeluarkan dibatalkan setakat ini.

Pada Selasa, Zahid mempertahankan kenyataannya bahawa penangguhan atau pembatalan SST bagi projek-projek terbabit adalah tepat, sambil menyatakan kesediaannya mengemukakan bukti dokumen mengenai arahan rasmi berkenaan.
Hari ini, RSN Rayer (PH-Jelutong) mendesak Zahid mengemukakan surat yang menyatakan bahawa projek pembangunan luar bandar di Sabah dan Sarawak itu telah dibatalkan.

After searching for ways to make money, he discovered that people online would pay for high quality copies of identity documents. Nazarenko got into the business of fake IDs.

“When you zoom in several hundred percent, you begin to understand how complicated even an ordinary passport or driver’s license really is. What looks like a simple plastic card to most people is actually made up of a huge number of small security and design elements,” he told me.

The ‘Ultimate’ $1,500 tier, meanwhile, let a customer upload a spreadsheet of the personal data they wanted to appear on the IDs, making the process even faster, and even came with a direct customer support representative on Telegram. He used LSD, magic mushrooms, and ecstasy. “That wasn’t about work anymore, it was about feeling something other than anxiety, about switching off a head that hadn’t switched off in years,” he said.

In early 2024, I discovered OnlyFake myself while scrolling through Telegram. I logged in, sent a small amount of cryptocurrency to the site, and generated some photos of fake IDs. I was blown away by the pictures of fake IDs laying on a carpet and upholstery. The implications for fraud were staggering, I thought. It seemed like it would shatter KYC practices — where cryptocurrency companies, for example, verify someone’s identity by having them upload a copy of their passport. What use is KYC when anyone can generate an identity document of essentially anyone else?

I entered the name David Creeks, put in a random birthday, and the site autofilled a bunch of other important information like the license’s issue and expiry dates. Just minutes later, I had photos of my California driver’s license laying on a rug. I made a British passport too.

After I made a couple of fake IDs with OnlyFake, I put them to the test. I successfully signed up for an account on OKX, a cryptocurrency exchange, using my fictitious ID. Former OKX employees later told me my test triggered a wave of changes inside the cryptocurrency exchange, who scrambled to make its systems more resilient to AI-generated IDs. (OKX did not respond to a request for comment for this story.)

While reporting that initial article, Abhishek Mathew, a cybersecurity researcher who followed the site’s growth, told me criminals were using OnlyFake to make bank accounts, or to unban their cryptocurrency accounts on Binance when asked for identification.

At the time, I messaged the administrator of OnlyFake, who went by the handle John Wick. Only now do I know that to be Nazarenko. Nazarenko, by then living at an apartment in Poland, said the generated photos could be used to bypass verification on all sorts of other sites, including Airbnb, Coinbase, and Revolut. Nazarenko also said, unconvincingly, “using our site for the purpose of forging documents is prohibited.”
At the time, the article received a lot of attention from researchers in the fraud world, and the public saw for the first just how AI could supercharge the creation of fake IDs.
With the article spreading, Nazarenko panicked. He deleted all of his personal emails, destroyed his laptop, and bought a new phone. He thought authorities would arrest him that very same day.

Nazarenko also made an announcement on the OnlyFake Telegram channel to his customers, and anyone else who might have taken a sudden interest in the site: “The news says that our generator was used to forge documents. This is complete nonsense. This has never happened before. At a minimum, because it cannot be used to forge documents.”

Charitably, perhaps Nazarenko was positing a deeply philosophical point about truth and reality: how can these documents be forgeries if the documents don’t actually exist? Really, he was covering his ass, fully aware he was offering a service that enabled criminals, and had been for years.

“At the time I hid behind ‘the client decides how to use it.’ That's a convenient thing to tell yourself so you don’t have to look at the real picture,” Nazarenko told me later. He knew that the documents he was creating could be used by someone to drain another person’s account, or launder money, or hide who they really were while doing all sorts of damage, he said.
After the article came out, the DDoS attacks against OnlyFake increased, Nazarenko said. He also received word that some very powerful people were taking advantage of his site.

On February 26, 2024, the United Nations wrote a letter to OnlyFake. It was on official UN letterhead, but OnlyFake, being a criminal enterprise, did not have a public office. So the UN sent a PDF of the letter to OnlyFake’s email account listed on the site.
“Dear Sir/Madam,” the letter, obviously not knowing who actually ran OnlyFake, started. “The Panel has received information that DPRK IT workers have utilized your service.”
The letter said that North Koreans had been using OnlyFakes to apply for remote work in the U.S.

As has been widely documented, thousands of North Koreans working for the regime got remote work jobs with U.S. companies, especially during the pandemic, and funnelled their wages back to North Korea to fund its nuclear weapon program. The UN letter said some of these workers were using OnlyFake to make fake IDs to sign up for freelance job sites, social media networks, and payment platforms. Alongside the country’s huge hacking campaigns against cryptocurrency exchanges, it was an ingenious way for North Korea to make more money.

The UN said it had information showing DPRK IT workers used OnlyFake to generate fake passports and driver’s licenses. Now, the UN wanted Nazarenko to hand over a ton of user data: a list of DPRK IT workers who had used OnlyFake; copies of all the documents OnlyFake had made for the DPRK; and what steps, if any, OnlyFake had taken to stop DPRK workers from using the site. (North Korean hackers recently stole $6.3 billion from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, in what is widely seen as one of the biggest hacks ever.)

The letter also addressed PassportCloud, a website that sold Photoshop templates of fake IDs and utility bills, and said North Koreans had used it to make fake bank statements and credit cards. I originally found OnlyFake after I first discovered PassportCloud and the sites appeared to be connected (one clue: it also used John Wick in its marketing). I asked Nazarenko multiple times if he was behind Passport Cloud too, but he never directly confirmed nor denied his involvement.

The UN demand was surreal to Nazarenko. He said he felt like he had only recently been working on a relatively small project. Now the UN was contacting him about how North Korean moles were probably using his service. He refused to give the UN anything, but looking back later, he said this is one of the first moments he realized he was in over his head. And for Nazarekno, it was about to get worse. A deeper threat was watching the growth of OnlyFake too: the FBI.

In May 2024, a few months after I published my article, a law enforcement agent working with prosecutors in the Southern District of New York went undercover. First, they bought a fake New York state identification card from OnlyFake, according to court records. Then they bought a fake U.S. passport card. Just over a week later, they purchased a New York state driver’s license and a U.S. passport. A couple of days later, they bought a fake Social Security card. OnlyFake, of course, happily provided all of these. OnlyFake’s customer support also told an undercover agent how best to use the fake IDs to circumvent KYC at cryptocurrency exchanges.

For someone who made a living protecting the identities of other criminals, Nazarenko had been very sloppy with his own security. When making the site and cashing out its proceeds, he sent Bitcoin to a cryptocurrency exchange account in his own name. Despite being a forger, he hadn’t bothered to make another identity.

It was trivial for authorities to identify who ran OnlyFake. Ukrainian authorities searched his parents’ house, Nazarenko said. Then on June 13, 2025, when Nazarenko flew to Bucharest, Romania, with his girlfriend for a friend’s birthday, the border officer took Nazarenko’s passport and spent an unusually long time looking at his computer. While being questioned in another room, authorities told Nazarenko there was a U.S. warrant out for his arrest. He was handcuffed, and for Nazarenko, everything “suddenly became very real.” Authorities seized some of OnlyFake’s servers too, Nazarenko said.

He spent three months in a Romanian prison before being extradited to New York. In Brooklyn’s Metropolitan Detention Center, prison officials transferred Nazarenko to another part of the facility when gang members assaulted him, according to a letter his lawyer later submitted in court.
“I was building something that could be used to harm people, and I was making money from it. I did not fully understand that until I was sitting inside a concrete cell,” Nazarenko said.

Igor Litvak, Nazarenko’s lawyer, said Nazarenko offered to cooperate with the authorities, including providing potential customers’ information. Litvak said he even showed the UN’s letter to the FBI, which indicated the sort of person who used this platform. But prosecutors didn’t take Nazarenko up on his offer. The U.S. Attorney’s Office in the Southern District of New York acknowledged a request for comment but did not respond to an email asking why authorities didn’t enter a cooperation arrangement with Nazarenko.

This June, around a year after his initial arrest, a judge sentenced Nazarenko to time served of 12 months, a remarkably light sentence compared to the maximum penalty of 15 years in prison. Perhaps this was due in part to the fact that authorities did not identify any specific victims of OnlyFake — only that the site existed and it was used to make IDs. For much of his time in prison, OnlyFake continued to be up and running, just with its owner locked away, Litvak said.

That wasn’t the end of Nazarenko’s time in detention, though. As he prepared to leave the court room, thinking his lawyer would immediately drive him to the airport so he could self-deport, ICE officials detained Nazarenko. He spent another two months in detention. “It was much, MUCH worse than prison,” Nazarenko said, referring to having to sleep on the floor and people dying in the facility.

On August 17, Nazarenko was deported along with several other Ukrainians on a chartered flight. When he finally walked out of the airport in Poland, then was taken by land to Ukraine, he had only what he was holding. “Everything’s gone, and I’m still here,” he remembered thinking. Nazarenko said he was then taken to a military enlistment office and drafted for the war. He says he escaped, left Ukraine on foot, and then flew eventually to Thailand.

203b9ab000261cac: The Excel copy-and-paste bug is back, which means Microsoft is making a second round of fixes.

The bug first appeared in the September update and manifested in multiple versions of Excel as a silent failure of the paste operation. Users copied content and attempted to paste it, but the destination cell was unchanged no matter how hard they mashed the Ctrl+V keys. Microsoft fixed it in mid-September. But it made a comeback in Excel 2016 when users installed October's security update.

Microsoft has now released a new build of Excel 2016 to address the reintroduction of the bug: build 16.0.5574.1006. The company wrote: "The new build includes all security updates for Microsoft Excel 2016, and also fixes the issue that was reintroduced in 16.0.5574.1005, in which paste operations might fail if the workbook contains conditional formatting."
Microsoft did not explain how the bug slipped back in. Copy and paste is, after all, a niche bit of functionality.

Users reported the recurrence of the bug in October after the KB5002934 update was applied. Rolling back the update resolved the problem until Windows Update pushed the patch again. KB5002934 is a security update that resolves glitches including remote code execution and information disclosure vulnerabilities.

The problem affects only Excel 2016 and is not the result of the latest Windows security update. Rather, it was reintroduced in an Excel update delivered through Windows Update. A user in a Microsoft Excel forum said the issue had appeared on workstations throughout their organization. "What's frustrating is that this is the same issue we encountered before, which was supposedly fixed in a previous update. Now it's back, barely a few weeks later."

And now, at least, it appears to be fixed once again. Still, if Microsoft is determined to reintroduce bugs into Excel, perhaps it might also be tempted to bring back the Hall of Tortured Souls (a secret first-person 3D mini-game hidden inside Microsoft Excel for Windows 95) and populate it with the testers who managed to miss the issue's resurrection. ®

Mahkamah mendapati Lee telah berjanji secara peribadi untuk memulangkan RM570,000 yang dibayar oleh pelabur di bawah perjanjian usaha sama terbabit, sebelum mengatur sebahagian pembayaran berjumlah RM100,000.
Pertikaian itu berpunca daripada beberapa perjanjian yang dimeterai pada 2022 melibatkan Agrigrow, Supernova Legacy Sdn Bhd dan dua lagi plaintif.
Menerusi perjanjian itu, Agrigrow sepatutnya membuat pajakan kecil dan bersama-sama membangunkan 15 plot tanah di Hutan Simpan Bukit Lagong, Gombak, bagi tujuan penanaman durian komersial.

Beliau berkata, keadaan itu menimbulkan isu yang memerlukan perbicaraan penuh bagi menentukan liabiliti mereka.
M Gobinath mewakili Lee, manakala Derrick Oon dan Low Jia Yi bertindak bagi pihak Supernova serta dua lagi plaintif.

c484f4ee5eba69eb: PETALING JAYA: The Attorney-General’s Chambers (AGC) will file an application to review the Court of Appeal’s decision to acquit independent preacher Syed Shah Iqmal Syed Mohammad Shaiful, better known as Da’i Syed, of a rape charge.
In a statement, the AGC said the decision to seek a review was made after examining the grounds of judgment delivered by the Court of Appeal today.
The review application would be filed under Rule 105 of the Rules of the Court of Appeal 1994.

“The review application will be based on the legal principles, criteria and threshold established for the exercise of the Court of Appeal's review jurisdiction, as outlined in the Federal Court's decision in Asean Security Paper Mills Sdn Bhd v Mitsui Sumitomo Insurance (Malaysia) Bhd.

“Accordingly, the prosecution's submissions will focus on whether there are exceptional circumstances that meet the required legal threshold to warrant the court's consideration in exercising its review jurisdiction,” the AGC said.

The Court of Appeal, in a 2-1 majority decision, ruled in favour of Syed Shah Iqmal’s appeal. Justice Azman Abdullah, reading the majority decision, said the defence had succeeded in raising reasonable doubt and that the conviction was unsafe.
The court consequently set aside the 10-year prison sentence and three strokes of the cane imposed by the Shah Alam High Court.
Azman also said the sessions court and High Court had seriously misdirected themselves in finding Syed Shah Iqmal guilty.
The majority panel noted the defence’s submissions on the victim’s demeanour, before, during and after the incident, which showed that the sexual intercourse happened with consent.
Syed Shah Iqmal claimed trial to raping a 23-year-old woman at a room in a condominium in I-City, Section 7, Shah Alam, at about 1.35am on Sept 11, 2019.
4979b799f3859346: KUALA LUMPUR: The finance ministry will determine whether rural development projects whose letters of acceptance (SSTs) have been deferred can proceed, says deputy rural and regional development minister Rubiah Wang.
She said her ministry complied with the finance ministry’s decision to defer all SSTs yet to be issued, including those pending issuance and projects ready to be put out to tender.
“The finance ministry’s decision does not come with a timeline. There is no timeline and an SST is only valid for two to three months.

“This means that if we do not receive further approval from the finance ministry within six months, the ministry would have to cancel the project and restart the process from scratch,” she told the Dewan Rakyat.

Rubiah was responding to Chong Zhemin (PH-Kampar), who asked for confirmation that none of the rural development projects in Sabah had been cancelled but merely deferred because of the suspension of the SST issuance.
She explained that the finance ministry's reason for deferring the SSTs was it wanted to stabilise the rural and regional development ministry’s finances, particularly its allocations.
“We anticipate that this situation could persist for another two or three years if immediate action is not taken.
“Furthermore, under another guideline used in the 13th Malaysia Plan, projects that cannot be put out to tender or implemented within two years face a high risk of being cancelled,” Rubiah said.

Last month, deputy prime minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi told the Dewan Rakyat that some projects in Sabah and Sarawak approved for 2026 were shelved on the orders of the rural and regional development ministry’s secretary-general, although funds had been allocated.
Zahid, who is also the rural and regional development minister, said that even SSTs issued to contractors had been cancelled.

However, finance minister II Amir Hamzah Azizan said the government had only postponed issuing new letters until outstanding payments to contractors were settled, maintaining that no letters already issued had been cancelled.
Zahid on Tuesday defended his remarks that the postponement or cancellation of SSTs for the projects were accurate and that he was prepared to produce documentary evidence of the official directive.
RSN Rayer (PH-Jelutong) today demanded that Zahid produce the letter which states the rural development projects in Sabah and Sarawak had been cancelled.

6cd9d143645a49ec: Campaigners against datacenter expansion are planning two days of coordinated action across Europe on November 6 and 7, demanding an immediate moratorium on new large-scale developments.

Following the US midterm elections, where restrictions on massive AI server farms were prominent in the campaigns from candidates in both major parties, it's now Europe's turn. Over 100 groups across 15 European countries will protest the boom in bit barn building over the next couple of days.
As well as demonstrations, there will be public meetings, stalls, petitions, walking tours, cycle rides, poetry readings and other creative actions, the organizers say.
The coalition of groups has put up a website – stopdirtydatacentres.eu – with an interactive map allowing anyone to find information on the events taking place and where.

In the UK, there is a photocall planned at 8am on November 6 outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) in Whitehall Place in central London, but also a Community Day of Action the following day at London's Brick Lane, where a facility is planned on the site of the former Truman Brewery.

Also on November 7, there will be a "family event" at St Michaels & All Angels Church in Great Torrington, Devon, to highlight the massive 1.5 GW data campus and on-site battery energy storage that is planned for 850 acres of farmland near the town.

The planned actions are a response to growing concerns about the impact of the wave of new compute shed projects on local communities, public infrastructure, land, water and energy use, housing, jobs and the cost of living.
Such concerns won't have been helped by recent events, such as a Google subsidiary reportedly felling 250,000 trees illegally in Finland to clear the ground for a server hall.

The campaigners claim that governments, the European Union and the tech giants are gambling with the future by racing ahead with server farm developments without proper scrutiny of the environmental, democratic and social impacts they might have.
A recent report found that businesses and private-sector trade associations dominated meetings with UK ministers to discuss datacenters, while environmental groups didn't get a look-in.

Campaigners are calling for an immediate moratorium on new large-scale projects across Europe, until clear frameworks are in place to determine whether new facilities should be built and under what conditions, with proper scrutiny and meaningful public participation.

"Datacenter developers in the UK and Europe want to cash in on the AI goldrush whatever the consequences. But communities everywhere are fighting back, seeing through Big Tech's PR machine and calling this what it is – a massive grab of scarce land, water and power resources by Silicon Valley billionaires," said Oliver Hayes, Head of Campaigns at Global Action Plan (UK).

"With governments failing to answer very basic questions about how many datacenters we need, what for, where, and how pollution will be avoided, the only reasonable course of action is an immediate moratorium," he said in a supplied remark.

They are unlikely to get much sympathy from the British government, which has pegged its hopes for economic growth on AI and wants more bit barns built to fulfil this. It has already used its powers to overturn rejections of planning permission for server farm projects by local councils.
Omdia analyst Alan Howard argues that datacenters also became a convenient political target during the US campaigns.
"The datacenter industry took a big hit in the US midterm elections which is quite disappointing, but not that surprising," Howard told The Register.

"The anti-datacenter rhetoric accelerated 12 months ago and in the last six months skyrocketed. While there have been many catalysts to point our fingers at, datacenters turned into an opportunistic political football. To be blunt, there is no shortage of politicians willing to exploit any opportunity to win an election and the datacenter 'problem' showed up just at the right time for this election."

Planned actions across Europe include events in Ireland, Poland, Denmark, Finland, Spain, the Netherlands, France, and the UK. A march to the Scottish Parliament in Edinburgh is also pegged for the following weekend, November 14. ®

fed1c46cfbab19f3: SHAH ALAM: A businessman has been ordered to repay RM470,000 to three investors after a proposed durian plantation venture in Selangor failed to materialise.
Judicial Commissioner Anita Harun, of the Shah Alam High Court, upheld a summary judgment against Lee Beng Tiong, but set aside the order against two other partners of Agrigrow Enterprise.
The court found that Lee had personally promised to refund the RM570,000 paid by the investors under the joint venture agreements and had subsequently arranged a partial repayment of RM100,000.
The dispute arose from agreements signed in 2022 involving Agrigrow, Supernova Legacy Sdn Bhd and two other plaintiffs.
Under the agreements, Agrigrow was to sublease and jointly develop 15 plots of land at the Bukit Lagong forest reserve in Gombak, for commercial durian cultivation.
However, the plaintiffs alleged that the plots were never delivered and rescinded the agreements. They also demanded a refund.
With RM470,000 still unpaid, they sued the three members of the partnership in the Selayang sessions court.
On April 29, the sessions court granted summary judgment against all three partners, holding them jointly and severally liable for the outstanding amount.
The partners appealed to the High Court, which today allowed the appeal in part.

Anita said the two other partners had joined Agrigrow only in February 2023, after the agreements were signed, and were not involved in Lee's promise to refund the money or Agrigrow's obligations under the agreements.
She said these circumstances raised issues that required a full trial to determine their liability.
M Gobinath represented Lee, while Derrick Oon and Low Jia Yi appeared for Supernova and the other two plaintiffs.

f516901f9e60d103: JAKARTA: An Indonesian police probe into the wiretapping of president Prabowo Subianto's phone was a matter for law enforcement, the country's police chief said on Thursday, as the scandal exposed the deepening cracks between Prabowo and his former backer and predecessor, Joko Widodo.

"We assure you that this is purely law enforcement and has nothing to do with rivalries or anything else," police chief Suyudi Ario Seto told reporters without elaborating, adding that the arrests must serve as a lesson for the police.

Prabowo took office in 2024 after winning the election in a landslide as the continuity candidate for Widodo, known also as Jokowi, whose son Gibran Rakabuming Raka was also elected as Prabowo's vice-president.

After details of the wiretapping scandal emerged, several lawmakers said on Thursday they were considering launching a parliamentary inquiry into Gibran's eligibility to serve after questions were raised about his election credentials, a move analysts saw as the first step to potentially remove him from office.
The wiretapping involved a Jokowi loyalist, and a spokesman for Prabowo said intercepting the president's communications could amount to treason.

Three senior police officers were arrested on Tuesday, including former national police chief and Prabowo's chief of staff, Listyo Sigit Prabowo, for allegedly tapping the phones of Prabowo as well as other politicians, journalists, civil society organisations, government officials, and business people since 2025.
Prabowo sacked Listyo, widely known as a Widodo loyalist, the next day.
The scandal has piled more pressure on the president, with public discontent growing over his costly populist policies and weakening investor confidence in Indonesia's US$1.5 trillion economy.
Neither the government nor police investigators have yet disclosed the motives behind the wiretapping.
Jokowi told reporters on Thursday that he respected the legal process.
Potential impreachment of VP

Political parties have started discussions to invoke parliament's right to hold an inquiry into the vice-president following the wiretapping case, said Hasto Kristiyanto, a senior official with the Indonesian Democratic Party of Struggle, the biggest party in parliament and the only one outside of Prabowo's coalition.

They are following up on rulings by the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court that Gibran's foreign senior high school credentials did not meet domestic legal requirements for vice-presidential candidates, and had been improperly accepted by election officials in 2024.
"There's increasingly intensive dialogue in the parliament to invoke their constitutional rights, especially after the wiretapping," Hasto said.
Three other parties in parliament - all within Prabowo's coalition - were also considering an inquiry into the matter, party officials said.
Under the constitution, lawmakers can launch an investigation into allegations of legal or constitutional violations by the government.
"We are currently reviewing these options and also communicating with other political parties," said Muhammad Kholid, a senior official of the Prosperous Justice Party.
The vice-president's office did not respond to a request for comment.
Prabowo's coalition controls 81% of parliament. Neither Jokowi nor Gibran belongs to a party represented in parliament.
Burhanuddin Muhtadi, a senior visiting fellow at Singapore's Yusof Ishak Institute, said the inquiry process would likely lead to Gibran's impeachment.

"It's ultimately leading to Gibran's impeachment, and some think they no longer need to do an investigation because there are already rulings from two courts," he said, adding that it looks increasingly unlikely that Jokowi and Prabowo would mend their relationship.

e41e66670bedc0b1: LONDON, Nov 5 — The makers of an Indian blockbuster based on the ancient Hindu epic Ramayana have hailed the new film as an unprecedented fusion of homegrown and Hollywood talent, calling it India’s first truly global release.
Ramayana: Rise of a Legend — in cinemas worldwide from Thursday — has been more than a decade in the making, with a reported mega US$420 million (RM1.7 billion) combined budget.
It draws on the talents of Oscar winners in visual effects and music, buoyed by a stellar cast featuring some of Indian cinema’s biggest names.
“People from all over the world came in to work on this project,” Bollywood superstar Ranbir Kapoor told AFP in London before its release.
“So we really had the platform to really express (ourselves) in the best way possible.”

The film, inspired by the millennia-old Sanskrit epic that serves as a foundational text for Hindus, chronicles the virtuous Rama’s (Kapoor) battle to save his kidnapped wife Sita from the evil demon king Ravana, played by fan-favourite Yash, who goes by one name.
This latest screen adaptation featuring flying elephants and gargantuan-sized demons is bursting with computer-generated visual effects, known in the industry as VFX.
The brainchild of producer Namit Malhotra, his UK-headquartered visual effects arm DNEG has won eight Academy Awards for work on films including Inception and Dune.

The movie, which has Hindi and English versions, has been scored by Oscar-winning composers Hans Zimmer and A.R. Rahman, while its action directors and production designers boast numerous Hollywood credits.
Planned as a two-part spectacle, the creators believe it heralds a breakout moment globally for India’s film industry, which has yet to win an Oscar in the coveted film categories.
‘Authentically Indian’
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This photo taken on April 29, 2026 shows Namit Malhotra, CEO of Double Negative (DNEG), a film special effects company, posing for a portrait at their London offices. — AFP pic
“It’s the largest production in the history of Indian cinema,” said Malhotra, who has branded it India’s Star Wars or Lord of the Rings.
“The story and the scale and the spectacle is something that the world, I think, is ready to consume.”
Long dominated by mass-market Hindi-language Bollywood, Indian cinema churns out around 2,000 films each year and has been expanding its global appeal.
That has been fuelled in part by the country’s strong diaspora networks and increasing access to Bollywood offerings on streaming platforms such as Netflix and Amazon Prime Video.
With its English version, Hollywood special effects and epic battle scenes, Ramayana appears aimed at international audiences as much as the movie-mad country of 1.4 billion people.

Made by Malhotra’s Mumbai-based Prime Focus Studios and actor Yash’s Monster Mind Creations, with Sony Pictures the international distributor, it eschews some hallmarks of traditional Bollywood, in particular its elaborate song-and-dance routines.
But many of Bollywood’s core ingredients — melodrama, romance and action alongside awe-inspiring landscapes and a long running time of nearly three hours for the English version — are present.
“It’s a very original telling of a very original story from India, and it makes no compromises in that regard. It keeps it authentically Indian,” Malhotra said.
Yash, a hugely popular figure in India’s Kannada-language cinema who co-produced and co-stars in Ramayana, told AFP that “East and West have come together in a true sense”.
The release and its global nature were “a very important moment” for Indian cinema, he added.
‘Personal connection’
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Moviegoers stand in a queue to watch the early morning show of the Indian Hindi-language epic mythological film ‘Ramayana:Part 1’, at the Miraj Cinemas in Mumbai on November 5, 2026. A big-budget film adaptation of the Ramayana, one of Hinduism’s most revered epics, has renewed attention on the ancient tale that continues to shape India’s culture, identity and politics. — AFP pic
In the film, Sita, played by South Indian star Sai Pallavi, is a fearless, fighting character.
She and other cast members highlighted the responsibility they felt in their roles, since many Indians have “a very personal connection with these characters”.
“It was quite challenging because you have to silence every part of you that wants to overperform and... let the character speak for itself,” Pallavi told AFP.
The filmmakers constructed a massive set in Mumbai for the central story settings, while VFX teams worked there and in London and Vancouver.
Although the movie was shot entirely in Hindi, the creators wrote an English-language screenplay for the global release.
English dialogue was added to a separate master version using both the cast and voice artists and traditional lip syncing techniques.
For director Nitesh Tiwari, evoking the ancient poem’s messaging was paramount.
“There’s a certain sense of timelessness to the emotions and the values which Ramayana stands for and that is exactly what we wanted to bring to the rest of the world,” he said. — AFP
