c064ec7bcbb77124: Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).
The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).

The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which was developed by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs and Honeygain were reorganized as independent platforms under an umbrella entity called Source, which received $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion.

Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.

Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.
The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

Likewise, Synthient’s report observes that the MECOOL set-top boxes exploded in popularity after the product was mentioned in 2023 by the Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips, which has an audience of nearly 17 million subscribers [Linus Tech Tips said in a statement shared with Synthient that it has since updated the video to explicitly frame the product as a scam and have removed all associated affiliate links].
The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”
Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”
“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”

Update, Nov. 5, 11:07 a.m. ET: In a statement shared post-publication, Oxylabs said that while its system is built so that a device can’t be used as a proxy exit node unless they receive a signal that it has consented, the developer faked these signals.

“We have been conducting regular audits of the applications provided by our partners,” the statement reads. “However, following this incident, we will improve the application and application’s build fingerprinting logic to better detect cases where the SDK is running on an unapproved build of an originally authorized application.”

The statement said Oxylabs has no record of any company called Videostrong Technology Co., but it did find between is suppliers the domain “com.abc[.]nexus,” mentioned in the GTIG report as an external malware loader.

“As soon as we saw that, we suspended the relationship and sent them a formal legal inquiry,” the statement reads. “This supplier accounts for less than 1% of our IP address pool. We had a signed contract with them, they assured our QA team that users had given consent, and we saw the consent flow ourselves.”
Further reading: Plume Security Labs white paper on the XCPE botnet (PDF) Black Lotus Labs writeup on LinkedIn TrendAI’s analysis Synthient’s list of affected devices, broken down by model number
9de50d9e2df39599: Baru-baru ini calon muda Pakatan Harapan (PH) bagi kerusi Kuala Linggi pada PRN Melaka, menarik perhatian ramai apabila mendakwa berjaya membantu menyelesaikan masalah penalti cukai lebih RM70,000 yang menghimpit sebuah persatuan nelayan sejak beberapa tahun lalu. Kemudian calon tersebut mengisytiharkan ‘This is how Gen Z works (beginilah cara Gen Z bekerja)’.

Kenyataan itu mengundang pelbagai reaksi. Penyokong parti menyatakan inilah generasi yang kita mahu, muda dan pantas tidak seperti pemimpin tua yang lambat, malas dan banyak main politik. Penyokong parti lawan pula sudah pastilah mentertawakan dan memperlekehkan kenyataan tersebut. Katanya 'budak ini' berangan.

Dakwaan calon tersebut menggambarkan seolah-olah selama ini orang tua tidak mampu menjadi pelaksana yang berkesan. Memang di media sosial pun sering kita lihat warga Malaysia bawah 60 tahun menyatakan rasa muaknya melihat muka pak cik-pak cik di Parlimen yang telah pun mereka lihat sejak kecil lagi. Sebab itu selalu timbul saranan agar kita tolak pemimpin tua dalam pilihan raya.

Soalannya, apakah sekarang kita benar-benar perlukan orang muda sebagai peneraju barisan hadapan dalam pentadbiran negara? Dan kali ini calon Gen Z sendiri telah mengangkat dirinya dan mendakwa generasinya mampu mengambil alih kerja ini dengan lebih efisien.

Di Threads sering saya lihat Gen Z bertekak dengan Gen Y (milenial). Masing-masing mahu membuktikan generasi merekalah paling bagus. Maksudnya, kami Gen X dan Boomers ni kira dinosaurlah, kena duduk di tepi diam-diam.

Tapi benar, memang perkembangan dunia hari ini sedang menyaksikan kebangkitan politik anak muda. Di Nepal, demonstrasi besar-besaran pada September 2025 yang digerakkan anak muda akibat kemarahan terhadap rasuah, nepotisme dan sekatan media sosial akhirnya membawa kepada kejatuhan kerajaan. Pada Mac 2026, Balendra Shah, bekas penyanyi rap berusia 35 tahun muncul sebagai perdana menteri baharu negara itu. Walaupun Shah sendiri tergolong dalam Gen Y, naiknya dia sebagai perdana menteri tidak dapat dipisahkan daripada gelombang perubahan yang digerakkan oleh Gen Z.

Di Kenya, anak muda bangkit menentang dasar percukaian dan tekanan ekonomi. Di Madagascar, anak muda bangkit melawan kerajaan. Di Maghribi menyaksikan gerakan bernama 'Gen Z 212' mendesak kerajaan melakukan pembaharuan pendidikan dan perkhidmatan kesihatan. Seperti kesan domino, walaupun tiada kaitan di antara mereka, kebangkitan anak muda ini semakin melebar ke serata dunia.

Paling baru bulan lepas dan masih berlaku, anak muda Perancis bangkit memprotes besar-besaran isu pendidikan sehingga memberikan tekanan kepada Presiden Emmanuel Macron. Gelombang rakyat kemudiannya menjadi makin besar dan merebak sehingga menarik penyertaan mahasiswa, kesatuan sekerja dan masyarakat umum memprotes isu-isu lain juga.

Ini memperlihatkan satu fenomena di mana golongan yang selama ini sering dianggap lembik dan cepat layu seperti strawberi tiba-tiba mampu mengucar-ngacirkan kestabilan politik sebuah negara. Apakah Malaysia juga sedang bergerak ke arah itu? Nampaknya calon Kuala Linggi ini cuba membayangkan bahawa proses pengambilalihan anak muda boleh bermula.

Melihat perkembangan dunia, kita tahu protes anak muda di jalan raya bukan perkara baru tetapi perlu ditegaskan bahawa menjatuhkan kerajaan dengan mentadbir kerajaan merupakan dua perkara berbeza. Semua orang boleh marah dan turun memprotes menumbangkan kerajaan. Semua orang boleh berceramah tetapi bukan semua boleh merangka dasar, merancang belanjawan dan mengurus ekonomi. Yang dulu kaki demo, kini sudah jadi menteri pun kita dapat lihat dia masih terpinga-pinga. Yang dah berhenti jadi menteri pun kita lihat banyak bercakap di podcast komplen sana-sini walhal sewaktu jadi menteri entah apa yang dia buat, tak nampak pun hasilnya.

Sebenarnya, kemunculan pemimpin muda bukan perkara baharu dalam sejarah politik negara kita. Najib Razak menjadi Ahli Parlimen ketika berusia 23 tahun, dilantik sebagai timbalan menteri pada usia 25 tahun dan menjadi menteri besar Pahang ketika berusia 29 tahun.

'Pengantin baru' Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman pun pernah menjadi menteri belia dan sukan pada usia 25 tahun. Kini, di kementerian sama menyaksikan Mohammed Taufiq Johari, menjawat jawatan menteri dalam usia tak sampai 30 tahun. Maknanya, kebolehan orang muda memimpin memang sentiasa diiktiraf. Bezanya dulu kita tidak melabelkan seseorang mengikut generasi yang bunyinya macam bunyi model telefon pintar atau kereta. Gen itulah, gen inilah!

Sebenarnya, saya sendiri rimas dengan label dan pembahagian kategori manusia kepada Baby Boomers, Gen X, Gen Y, Gen Z, Alpha dan bermacam-macam generasi lagi. Bagi saya, label tersebut bukanlah ketetapan saintifik yang mutlak. Label generasi yang pada asalnya digunakan dalam kajian sosial ini kemudian telah menjadi alat pemasaran dalam dunia perniagaan.

Dalam dunia pemasaran, pengguna perlu dikenal pasti, dikelompokkan supaya produk dapat dijual dengan lebih berkesan. Meletakkan label pada generasi adalah satu jalan mudah untuk tujuan tersebut. Masalah yang timbul ialah apabila kategori pemasaran ini mula dianggap sebagai kebenaran fakta tentang sifat manusia. Boomers beginilah, Gen X begitulah, kononnya mereka lebih lasak tapi menjadi hamba pekerjaan. Generasi sekarang pula lebih pintarlah, tetapi lembik macam strawberi. Macam saya kata tadi, kebenaran teori itu tidak mutlak dan bergantung kepada banyak faktor.

Padahal, perbezaan yang diperdebatkan selalu ini hanya sekadar pertembungan biasa antara golongan tua dengan orang muda. Orang muda dulu pun memberontak dan mempertikaikan kewibawaan orang tua yang dirasakan sudah mula tumpul. Kita waktu muda dahulu pun rebel, mahu bebas dan bercita-cita mengubah dunia. Manakala orang tua adatnya pula sentiasa meragui keupayaan anak muda. Macam kita hari ini berat untuk menyerahkan baton kerana menganggap anak muda masih belum cukup matang dan kurang pengalaman.

Di Malaysia pula, budaya politiknya memang sudah 'begitu' sejak sekian lama. Anak muda yang mahu menjadi pemimpin kebanyakannya masih perlu melalui struktur parti yang dikuasai generasi tua. Mereka perlu mendapat restu kepimpinan, mematuhi disiplin parti dan menyesuaikan diri dengan budaya politik sedia ada ini. Pendek kata, dengan acuan politik tua, Gen Z yang berada di dalamnya pun akan kelihatan poyo dan tak menarik. Itulah yang berlaku ketika Baby Boomers, Gen X dan milenial masih muda. Mahu mengubah, bercakap lantang tentang kebangkitan anak muda tetapi akhirnya tersedut ke dalam lubang yang sama.

Apakah boleh terjadi satu gelombang di mana anak muda Gen Z beramai-ramai menyertai mana-mana parti politik besar tanah air dan melakukan 'serang hendap' mengambil alih tampuk kepimpinan lama lalu melakukan reformasi politik? Sempatkah mereka naik atau belum apa-apa mereka semua akan dicantas?

Kepada calon Kuala Linggi, saya mengalu-alukan calon muda tetapi saya kira keberkesanan seseorang pemimpin bukan diukur dengan cepat atau lambatnya mendapat tandatangan perdana menteri. Itu masih belum dianggap satu perubahan. Dan kalau itulah yang dikatakan sebagai satu kerja, ia bukanlah sesuatu yang membanggakan. Budaya surat sokongan, budaya potong barisan guna kabel politik bukan perkara baru dan bukan budaya yang sihat.

Jika Gen Z bercita-cita untuk melakukan reformasi, ia harus mempercekapkan sistem pentadbiran itu sendiri tanpa banyak kerenah birokrasi dalam menyelesaikan masalah rakyat. Jika itu berjaya, kita tak perlukan hubungan istimewa wakil rakyat dengan Perdana Menteri untuk meluluskan sebarang pekerjaan. Kita mahu kecekapan sistem itu sendiri yang memainkan peranan dengan berkesan. Itu yang harus anak muda Gen Z ubah jika berjaya menjadi perangka dasar di Dewan Rakyat.

Persoalan sama ada Gen Z mampu memimpin negara tidak boleh dijawab dengan melihat kad pengenalan, kepetahan berpidato, jumlah 'follower' TikTok atau aktif menghasilkan video. Kita memerlukan pemimpin yang memahami tanggungjawab, mempunyai keberanian membuat keputusan, menghormati institusi dan sanggup dipertanggungjawabkan apabila melakukan kesilapan. Ciri-ciri tersebut tetap ada pada sesetengah pemimpin tua kita hari ini. Sekiranya ada ahli politik dari Gen Z yang tidak memenuhi kriteria tersebut, pada saya dia hanyalah mesin baharu dengan program lama.

Sesebuah negara itu hebat kerana pemimpinnya sentiasa mempunyai idea segar, bertenaga dan bersemangat melaksanakan visinya tanpa mengira berapa pun usianya. Tetapi jika pemimpin generasi muda terus membawa perangai politik lama yang poyo dan main -main, nescaya kita tidak akan ke mana-mana. Harap muka sahaja muda, idea dan wawasannya tetap lapuk. Buat apa? Kepada calon muda Kuala Linggi, jika cita-cita anda memang mahukan perubahan, 'pak cik' sokong!

12205f0e791d641a: It will cut the bureacratic red tape that plagues state institutions
Originally published on Global Voices
Image by Sbunker. Used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

One of the biggest barriers for people’s effective engagement with the authorities in Kosovo is a confusing and unresponsive bureaucracy. Whenever citizens want to report a problem in their community, such as potholes or illegal waste disposal, they are met with a system that requires them to know the roles and responsibilities of various state institutions and handle necessary paperwork themselves.

When submitted to the wrong agency or without proper documents, citizens’ complaints are either ignored or can take long periods to be processed, which discourages engagement and has an adverse effect on people’s trust in the government. Ultimately, it deteriorates the already challenging situation regarding transparency, communication, and accountability of state bodies in Kosovo.

In 2026, a local non-governmental organization (NGO), Sbunker, responded to this challenge by creating an online platform called Kosovo.report to help citizens report their complaints to the authorities in a quick and easy manner. Global Voices conducted an email interview with Hana Deva, project manager at SBunker, to learn more about their initiative. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Hana Deva (HD): Sbunker is a non-governmental organization founded in 2016, focused on providing analysis and informed perspectives on important political, economic, social, and cultural issues in Kosovo and the Western Balkans.

Through our Disinfo program, we monitor local and regional media content to identify and address disinformation. Sbunker produces podcasts and other media content exploring political and social developments, philosophical, cultural, and theoretical discussions.

We joined the Digital Sparks project because we wanted to create a direct form of civic engagement through technology. This led to the development of Kosovo.report, a platform designed to give citizens a simple way to report problems and submit requests concerning their neighborhoods and local communities.
The platform is intended to act as a link between citizens and public institutions by helping these reports reach the relevant institutions and making the process more accessible to the citizens.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?
HD: Through our work in media and civic engagement, we became interested in how citizens communicate everyday problems in their communities to public institutions.

Research on public administration in Kosovo points to fragmented public service delivery, inconsistencies in administrative procedures and digital services, and continuing challenges in communication between citizens and institutions.
This can make the process of reporting an issue to the right department unclear.

Kosovo.report was developed with this challenge in mind. The idea is to give citizens a more straightforward way to report an issue, without requiring them to first determine which institution or department is responsible.
Based on the type and location of the problem, the platform is designed to route the report to the appropriate department and allow the citizen to follow what happens afterwards.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?
HD: Our main work has been the development of Kosovo.report, from the initial concept to a functional platform now being prepared for its pilot phase.

Alongside this development, we have coordinated with the Municipality of Prishtina to determine how reports should reach the appropriate departments, and prepared a Memorandum of Understanding to formalise this cooperation.

Beyond the platform, Sbunker has served as a capacity hub for other Digital Sparks project grantees during the project period. We organized meetings and an advocacy workshop where grantees worked on developing a joint advocacy event.

We also hosted a young fellow, Bora Dibra, from the Albanian organization IRSH (Young Intellectuals, Hope), for a one-month fellowship focused on digital civic engagement, media literacy, and participatory advocacy.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.
HD: The project has allowed Sbunker to expand the way we approach civic engagement. Much of our work traditionally focused on informing citizens and creating public debate through publications.

Through Kosovo.report, we are developing a tool that takes this a step further by giving citizens a channel through which they can raise problems in their communities and have their reports directed to the relevant departments.
The next step will be the pilot of Kosovo.report in the capital, Prishtina, where we will be able to test the platform with citizens, gather their feedback, and identify what needs to be improved.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?
HD: Developing Kosovo.report has given us experience in creating a digital tool through which citizens can report issues and direct them to the relevant departments.

The process has also involved working with the Municipality of Prishtina as we prepare for the pilot phase of the project, which is a different scope of work from Sbunker's focus on media and public debate.

Our role as a capacity hub has also given us an opportunity to work more closely with individual grantees and other civil society organizations, learn about their projects in digital democracy, and the challenges in their communities.

Taken together, these activities have expanded Sbunker’s experience from media, analysis and public debate, to developing digital tools and working more closely with civil society organizations and public institutions.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

HD: One of the most valuable experiences has been developing something that is intended to have a direct use in people’s everyday lives. With Kosovo.report, we are taking a different approach by developing a platform that citizens can use in their communities and communicate with relevant institutions.
Building the platform has also given us a better sense of what it takes to turn an idea for civic participation into something that works in practice.
The capacity hub and fellowship have added to this experience by allowing us to work with people approaching digital democracy and civic engagement from different projects and contexts.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

HD: For us, Kosovo.report is a starting point for what we want to do in the digital democracy area. The current focus is on Prishtina, but we want to take the platform beyond the pilot and explore opportunities to connect with other municipalities and public institutions across Kosovo.
The first phase is helping us see what works, what needs to be improved, and how the platform can better respond to the needs of local communities.

The project has also strengthened Sbunker’s capacity to develop digital approaches to civic participation. We want to build on that experience in our future work by looking more closely at the needs of the communities we work with and explore where digital tools can help address them.
We also want to continue the relationships developed through this project, both with civil society organizations and collaborators, and see where they can lead beyond the project.

1a7942fb3b9f842f: Diplomacy is not always measured by grand agreements, historic handshakes or comprehensive peace settlements.
Sometimes, its effectiveness is demonstrated through small but tangible improvements in human lives.
The recent decision by Myanmar’s military authorities to begin releasing ethnic Rakhine deportees following Malaysian diplomatic pressure is one such development.
According to The Irrawaddy, the releases followed Malaysia’s intervention over the detention of individuals deported from Malaysia to Myanmar.
This is hardly a diplomatic breakthrough. Yet it is not insignificant.
It demonstrates that Putrajaya’s decision to maintain engagement with Nay Pyi Taw, despite international criticism, can produce limited but measurable results.
More baby steps are needed.
First, engagement must never be confused with endorsement.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has faced criticism for engaging Myanmar’s military leadership, particularly Senior General now President Min Aung Hlaing.
Critics argue that such engagement risks legitimising a regime responsible for widespread displacement, military violence and the destruction of democratic institutions.
These concerns are valid.

However, refusing to communicate with the authorities exercising power in Nay Pyi Taw would make it harder for Malaysia to secure detainees’ release, negotiate humanitarian access or protect vulnerable returnees.
Diplomacy requires contact, even with governments whose conduct one fundamentally opposes.
The purpose is not to confer legitimacy but to influence behaviour.
Second, the releases demonstrate the potential value of sustained diplomatic pressure.
Malaysia raised concerns about the treatment of its deportees. Foreign minister Mohamad Hasan sought clarification. Myanmar subsequently began releasing those detained.
Although this sequence does not prove that Malaysian pressure alone led to the releases, it suggests that diplomatic intervention mattered.
Malaysia did not merely accept Myanmar’s treatment of the deportees. It demanded accountability.
This is how engagement should function: dialogue accompanied by expectations, verification and humanitarian safeguards.
Third, piecemeal progress must not conceal Myanmar’s larger humanitarian catastrophe.
Without a doubt, Myanmar remains deeply fractured.
The military authorities do not exercise uncontested control over the entire country.
Ethnic armed organisations and resistance forces remain powerful actors.
Rakhine State is particularly complicated because of the continuing conflict involving the Arakan Army and Myanmar’s military.
Repatriation cannot automatically be considered safe merely because some detainees have been released.
Malaysia must distinguish between voluntary returns and deportations that expose vulnerable people to persecution, detention or forced recruitment.
The principle of non-refoulement must remain central.
Fourth, Malaysia needs stronger mechanisms to monitor returnees.
Diplomatic assurances are meaningful only when independently verified.
Malaysia should work with relevant UN agencies and humanitarian organisations to establish procedures for monitoring the welfare of those returned.
Such arrangements should protect family contact, freedom from arbitrary detention and access to humanitarian assistance.
Without verification, Malaysia risks celebrating releases without knowing whether those individuals subsequently enjoy meaningful security.
Fifth, Asean must translate Malaysia’s incremental progress into collective diplomatic action.
To be sure, the Asean Five-Point Consensus has struggled to end Myanmar’s conflict.
Nevertheless, its fundamental objectives remain relevant: reducing violence, encouraging inclusive dialogue and facilitating humanitarian assistance.
Malaysia’s bilateral engagement should complement these objectives, not replace them.
The Philippines, as Asean Chair in 2026, should consider how such diplomatic openings can strengthen regional cooperation.
Asean needs more than repeated expressions of concern.
It needs Asean’s resolve to translate principles into practical humanitarian outcomes.
Sixth, engagement must extend beyond Myanmar’s military leadership.
Malaysia should maintain communication with the National Unity Government (the Myanmar government-in-exile), ethnic armed organisations, civil society and humanitarian networks.
Myanmar’s fragmentation makes broader engagement indispensable.
A settlement negotiated exclusively with military authorities cannot guarantee acceptance throughout the country.
Malaysia must broaden and deepen its diplomatic channels without abandoning humanitarian principles.
Finally, Anwar’s approach should be judged by outcomes rather than appearances.
Malaysia cannot single-handedly resolve Myanmar’s civil war.
But neither should it abandon opportunities to secure modest improvements in human security.
The release of Rakhine deportees is encouraging, although it does not establish that Myanmar has fundamentally changed.
Further progress requires humanitarian access, independent monitoring, safeguards for returnees and eventually inclusive political dialogue.
Myanmar’s crisis cannot be resolved overnight. Yet diplomatic paralysis is not a strategy.
Malaysia must remain principled without becoming immobilised by the complexity of Myanmar’s conflict.
The journey towards peace may begin with small humanitarian concessions rather than spectacular diplomatic breakthroughs.
More baby steps are needed. But genuine, verifiable and sustainable piecemeal progress is still progress.
For Myanmar’s long-suffering people, even modest improvements in human security matter.

de929831445c05d5: Walaupun seminggu sudah berlalu saya terpanggil menulis mengenai Perjanjian Keyakinan dan Perbekalan dimeterai antara kerajaan, Ahli Parlimen Bersatu, bekas Ahli Parlimen parti itu yang menyokong PMX dan Ahli Parlimen Muar Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman.

Wakil Ummo jadi perdana menteri yang dimaksudkan kita tahu ialah Ismail Sabri Yaakob. Apa yang berlaku? Tentu ramai masih ingat. Pada September 2021, Ismail memeterai apa yang dipanggil memorandum persefahaman dan kestabilan politik dengan Anwar Ibrahim yang waktu itu ketua pembangkang.
Kata Anwar, memorandum itu menjadi kenyataan kerana sikap positif Ismail yang mengambil pendekatan berunding segera dengan pembangkang sebaik dilantik perdana menteri kesembilan.

Perlu dinyatakan memorandum itu bukan CSA per se. Ini diakui Anwar sendiri waktu itu. Zahid konon mahu Ismail strike while the iron is still hot.

Tekanan demi tekanan dikenakan ke atas Ismail. Menyulitkan Ismail ialah beliau sekadar seorang naib presiden Umno manakala Zahid presiden parti . Akhirnya, Ismail tidak ada pilihan melainkan tunduk akur. Parlimen dibubarkan pada Oktober 2022 dan PRU15 diadakan pada November 2022.
Dan Umno/BN mencatat prestasi paling buruk dalam sejarah mereka. Umno hanya menang 27 kerusi, MCA (2) dan MIC (1). Perkiraan Zahid meleset.

Fast forward CSA yang dimeterai 29 Okt lalu. Pada upacara tandatangan kerajaan diketuai Timbalan Perdana Menteri II Fadillah Yusof. Bukan timbalan perdana menteri I. Kita tahu siapa pemegang jawatan itu.
Mungkinkah ini kerana pendirian lalu Zahid terhadap MoU 2021 dan tindakan susulannya yang boleh dilihat sebagai bertentangan dengan semangat MoU itu?
Maka, kerana itulah saya tersenyum lebar seperti disebut tadi apabila Zahid memuji CSA 2026 dan mahu ia diperluas kepada semua parti.

b91db1d100bf604d: Utilizing waste carbon at scale, assessing public trust in artificial intelligence and data centers, and building a quantum toolkit for critical applications were among the topics energy experts explored at the MIT Energy Initiative (MITEI)’s annual research conference on Sept. 22-23. The complexity of the energy transition demands “a truly interdisciplinary and international approach,” said Paula Hammond, Institute Professor and dean of the MIT School of Engineering, kicking off the conference, which was themed “Transitioning energy at a pivotal moment.”  More than 200 people attended Energizing@MIT: MITEI’s Annual Research Conference in person and online, including faculty, scientists, and researchers; representatives of global energy firms; nonprofit organizations; and academic institutions. With the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence and data centers, the challenge of the energy transition grows ever greater, requiring “researchers who can pursue fundamental questions about materials, chemistry, and energy systems … engineers who can design new technologies and determine how they might function at scale … and experts in economics, policy, human behavior, and sociology who can help us understand how those technologies will interact with communities and with the world around us,” said Hammond.  From keynote speakers to panelists, seed grant innovators to startup entrepreneurs, the conference featured exemplars in all these categories. Deploying today’s technologies Eric Toone, chief technical officer and managing partner at Breakthrough Energy, set the tone for day one with a keynote address that was clear-eyed in his assessment. “If energy is prosperity,” he told the audience, “at least today, prosperity is emissions.” Yet, Toone was optimistic when he heralded examples of Breakthrough Energy-funded ventures, from iron-air batteries to vacuum-insulated glass windows, which can reduce the carbon costs of energy.  “We can absolutely develop new technologies that provide the exact same service, but at zero carbon,” he said. The conference made Toone’s claim tangible as it spanned the full arc of decarbonization — from deploying what we know today to uncovering what may be possible tomorrow.  There are “projects that are actually being developed, companies that are putting steel in the ground now, electrons onto the grid to deliver capacity now, or in the very, very near term,” said John Parsons, deputy director for research at the MIT Center for Energy and Environmental Policy Research. Parsons moderated a panel on the revival of nuclear fission power.  Highlights included Crane Clean Energy Center’s restoration of the Three Mile Island Unit 1 nuclear plant, set to restart in mid-2027; work by Électricité de France (EDF) to extend and modernize France’s 57-reactor nuclear fleet, adapting plants to climate impacts; and GE Vernova’s development of mature light-water reactor technology, with a new plant under construction in Ontario. Carbon utilization offers another path to mitigating carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions. “The land and ocean are passively taking up almost 50 percent of anthropogenic CO2 emissions,” said Carolyn Ruppel, MITEI’s deputy director for science and technology, who moderated the panel. “The idea is to find uses for some of the rest of it.” The session showcased research exploring a host of technologies for making products with captured CO2. Nicola Ferralis, a research scientist in the MIT Department of Materials Science and Engineering (DMSE), highlighted the importance of large-scale uses for carbon waste, such as structural carbon for vehicles and buildings. “We need to find applications that are actually able to match the supply by mass,” he said.  Admir Masic, an associate professor in the MIT Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering and DMSE, described self-heating concrete panels used in real-world conditions in Sapporo, Japan, as well as new concrete materials that can store energy. “The pace of the transition to a renewable-energy economy will strongly rely on the availability of scalable, bulk energy-storage solutions,” said Masic. Kripa K. Varanasi, a professor in the MIT Department of Mechanical Engineering, is working on ways to make technologies such as emissions-plume capture at power plants economically viable.  In a panel devoted to startups with links to MITEI or MITEI member companies, speakers described moving novel energy technologies from research to commercialization: Alfredo Rivela of Adaion has developed an AI tool for electrical utilities that optimizes their use of the grid; Eddie Obropta of Raptor Maps trains drones to inspect solar farms; Michele Guarnieri’s HiBot has created a robot that detects issues in power lines; and Michael Wang of Lithios is conducting field pilots that use electrochemistry to separate lithium from low-grade brines. Successful ventures, the speakers agreed, begin with a clear customer problem that can be validated by industry users and that offers a path to scaled deployment. For industry users, “innovation is not a corporate virtue,” said Steve Hellman, managing partner at Alliance Partners. “It’s an existential requirement.” Early-stage research and basic science The conference also offered a bounty of promising early research on technologies and approaches for cutting carbon emissions. A panel on MITEI’s Seed Innovation Fund Program projects introduced MIT scientists who are separating and recycling rare earth elements; designing algorithms to decide which power plants should run to meet electricity demand; and modeling the impacts on human and natural systems of development and decarbonization. A poster session revealed the next generation of energy researchers in such fields as chemistry, architecture, aeronautics and astronautics, and computer science. Graduate students are developing a wide array of technologies for carbon mitigation and new energy systems, such as a steam electrolysis process for hydrogen production; models of end-to-end decarbonization in buildings; and designs for hydrogen- and methane-fueled aircraft. The conference highlighted the importance of fundamental science in feeding the pipeline of new energy technologies. Wednesday’s keynote speaker, Danna Freedman, the F. G. Keyes Professor of Chemistry at MIT and inaugural director of the MIT Quantum Initiative (QMIT), traced scientists’ evolving capacity to harness quantum computing as a tool for solving a range of problems, including those in energy. “What we want to do at QMIT is solve the hard problem, and the hard problem isn’t developing these ridiculously intricate and beautiful quantum tools,” said Freedman. “It is connecting the quantum tools with the applications that will change the world.” A companion panel explored one such application: quantum sensing, which leverages fundamental physics to capture a nanoscale view of materials and their properties. For instance, Lukasz Zielinski, scientific advisor to the Integrated Sensing and Measurement Program at SLB, uses a lidar camera with single-photon detectors to identify methane plumes. Moderator Paola Cappellaro, the Ford Professor of Engineering in the MIT Department of Nuclear Science and Engineering, described her work using diamond-based sensors for detecting tiny magnetic fields from battery current, potentially helping measure battery conditions without disturbing the battery electrically. Such quantum sensors, Cappellaro said, can be “practical and impactful.”  Data centers and public trust One critical challenge facing energy researchers and industry emerged in sessions throughout the two days: the explosive growth of AI and the energy-hungry data centers that fuel this technology. As Deepjyoti Deka, a MITEI principal research scientist, put it, “the big test for AI right now is whether AI can reduce energy usage, improve efficiency, as well as bring in innovation faster than the rate at which it is going to consume electricity to get trained and deployed.”  “New ‘hyperscale’ facilities built for artificial intelligence can use more power than entire cities,” said Steve Clemmer, director of energy research in the Climate and Energy Program at the Union of Concerned Scientists, sharing a recent analysis of data center proliferation. With new facilities being 10 to even 10,000 times larger than data centers built just a decade ago, he said, wholesale electricity costs will rise, and “increased reliance on fossil fuels will result in tens of billions of dollars in health damages, and trillions in climate damages.” He noted that decision-makers can mitigate these harmful impacts through clean energy development, strong ratepayer protections, and other safeguards. Given mounting opposition to data centers, Kathryn Kline Tyndall, associate director of energy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, recommended that industry proponents provide early, accessible information about power, water, quality-of-life, land-use, environmental, and economic impacts, tailored to each community in which they hope to set up shop. Larry Susskind, the Ford Professor of Urban and Environmental Planning in the MIT Department of Urban Studies and Planning, recommended that developers go further, and demonstrate credible benefits to communities. To achieve this, Susskind suggests a facilitated negotiation process between developers and local groups whose object is a community benefits agreement — a deal that might involve altering the data center design, and providing workforce development, infrastructure investment, and clean energy partnerships. Ultimately, developers must accept that they can’t rush community acceptance; they have to earn it by giving residents a meaningful role in shaping projects and sharing their benefits.  “You’re going to have to proceed at the speed of trust,” said Susskind.

ac22cefe62ba9640: Internet rights advocates and Lula da Silva campaigners challenge Meta’s alleged shadow banning
Originally published on Global Voices
Screenshot from the naosemeta.com.br landing page. Fair use.

This story is part of Undertones, Global Voices’ Civic Media Observatory’s newsletter and column. Subscribe to Undertones here. It is also part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.
Over the years, Meta’s content moderation policies and governance practices have faced intense scrutiny and legal challenges over alleged political bias and a lack of transparency.

Since 2018, the Arab Center for Social Media Advancement (7amleh), a human rights organization advocating for Palestinian digital rights, has documented how Facebook’s (now Meta) moderation practices disproportionately affect Palestinian content. In 2020, 7amleh launched a campaign challenging Facebook’s proposed hate speech policy, which considered “Zionist” a potential proxy for “Jew” or “Jewish.” More recently, in 2024, the organization collected 20 first-hand testimonies from Palestinian influencers, journalists, and media outlets documenting their experiences of Meta’s discriminatory content moderation practices. In 2023, Human Rights Watch also reported “systemic online censorship” against voices in support of Palestine and Palestinian human rights,

In 2022, Tom Vandendriessche, a Belgian politician and Member of the European Parliament (MEP) representing the far-right Vlaams Belang (Flemish Interest) party, partially prevailed in a legal case against Meta concerning a shadow ban imposed on his account in 2021 after the company removed several posts alleging a breach of its Terms of Service (ToS) and Facebook Community Guidelines (FCG). A Belgian court ordered the company to compensate the politician for financial and reputational damages, finding that its actions had significantly restricted his ability to engage in political discourse online and that Meta had failed to provide adequate transparency or effective avenues for redress.

In 2026, Meta has faced significant criticism in Brazil and internationally from internet rights watchdogs over political bias, algorithmic interference, and the selective suppression of content perceived as favoring far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro during the October 2026 Brazilian presidential election.
Narrative: Meta, take your hands off our election!

Using the slogan Meta não se meta (roughly, “Meta, stay out of it”), which plays on the Portuguese word meta, derived from the verb meter (“to get involved” or “to interfere”), internet rights defenders and current President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s followers and allies sought not only to expose alleged Meta’s shadow-banning practices during Brazil’s 2026 presidential election but also to mobilize Brazilians to demand a fairer digital space collectively.
Sub-narrative: We demand digital sovereignty, and we will hold Meta accountable

In October 2026, during the Brazilian presidential runoff election campaign, a coalition of Brazilian civil society organizations, social movements, and digital rights advocacy groups, including CTRL+Z, Código Não Binário, ARTIGO 19 (Article 19 Brasil), Sleeping Giants Brasil, and others, launched the webpage naosemeta.com.br as part of their initiative to denounce electoral interference and algorithmic bias. The site offered three ways for people to hold Meta accountable online: email Meta; message Meta’s General Director in Brazil on LinkedIn; and comment on Meta Ceo Mark Zuckerberg’s latest Instagram post. It also shared a space for those wishing to join and sign a petition to the Superior Electoral Court and an extrajudicial notification, a formal written communication sent on October 19 to put Meta on notice and demand that it recognize the technical flaws in its advertising, moderation, and artificial intelligence (AI) systems, and the distribution and availability of user-generated content and campaign materials in Brazil — which these organizations claim disadvantaged, in particular, candidate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

Screenshot of an Instagram post from Núcleo de Tecnologia do MTST. The video shows protesters in the demonstration held on October 19, 2026, in front of Meta to denounce the company's questionable moderation practices during Brazil's 2026 presidential election. Fair use.

The online strategy to hold Meta accountable was accompanied by a protest in front of Meta’s offices on October 19, where participants called for respect for Brazil’s digital sovereignty, with the Homeless Workers Movement’s Technology Center among the loudest voices.

For those reclaiming digital sovereignty, the company’s actions stem from the relationship between U.S. President Donald Trump and Brazil’s ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, father of Flávio Bolsonaro, and the influence the current U.S. administration has over big-tech owners — they consider Meta to be facilitating foreign interference.
Sub-narrative: Together, we can “tame” the algorithm

An extra layer supported the narrative “Meta, take your hands off our election!” After the first round of the election gave candidate Flávio Bolsonaro a small lead in early October, left-wing Congressman André Janones relaunched his WhatsApp channel, “Lula’s Army,” an initiative to mobilize voters online and offline and give visibility to Lula da Silva’s messaging and proposals, and that quickly gained millions of followers.
Screenshot of Lula's Army WhatsApp channel showing instructions to engage with content from Lula da Silva's campaign to boost it. Fair use.

In addition to reclaiming Brazilian symbols from the far-right, including inviting followers to wear the country’s yellow soccer team T-shirt, the WhatsApp channel coordinated social media interactions to boost Lula da Silva’s visibility. By giving his “troops” instructions on when and how to engage with the content Lula da Silva’s campaign produced, Janones positioned an implicit narrative that argued it was possible to “tame” the algorithm, regain ownership of the Brazilian digital media ecosystem, and ultimately win the election, recapturing the campaign spirits.

After Lula da Silva’s unprecedented second-round comeback on October 25, this narrative evolved to “dobramos a Meta,” which translates to “we doubled Meta,” hinting at the “dobrar a meta” (doubled the target) popular meme that originated from a statement made by former Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff in July 2015, during a speech on the National Program for Access to Technical Education and Employment (PRONATEC)— all to say “we were able to overcome Meta’s content moderation policies and governance.”
Screenshot of an Instagram post from CTRLZ showing the message “dobramos a Meta,” which translates to “we doubled Meta.” Fair use.
The context surrounding the narrative

Brazil ranks as the world’s second-largest country by WhatsApp users (148 million) and the third-largest addressable Instagram audience (147 million). The country is considered a pioneer in internet governance and digital regulation, with a strong tradition of open, multistakeholder approaches to protecting digital rights, especially thanks to the country's foundational internet law, Federal Law No. 12.965/2014, known as the Marco Civil da Internet.

For more than 10 years, Brazil’s Marco Civil da Internet protected digital platforms from civil liability for third-party content, except when they failed to comply with a specific court order requiring its removal, safeguarding freedom of expression while preventing platforms from being inundated with takedown requests. This changed in June 2025, when the country’s Supreme Court, recognizing shifts in digital media ecosystems, ruled that Federal Law No. 12.965/2014 was partially unconstitutional because it no longer sufficiently protected fundamental rights and democracy. The ruling made digital platforms liable for third parties’ content in Brazil, a decision experts argue is impossible to fulfill until digital platforms offer real transparency into their content moderation policies and governance practices.

In October 2026, Sleeping Giant Brasil shared a report on what they consider evidence of Meta’s “algorithmic favoritism” toward the Bolsonaros’ political allies, focusing on the case of Nikolas Ferreira, a right-wing politician affiliated with the Liberal Party (PL) — currently serving as a Member of the Chamber of Deputies, elected for a four-year term in 2022.

On October 14, the Brazilian independent news site Nucleo shared an investigation showing how Meta’s AI favored creating images of Flávio Bolsonaro on WhatsApp. According to the outlet, Meta acknowledged the failure via email and said it would take the necessary measures to prevent it from happening again.

On October 15, Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court (TSE) ruled that Meta must refrain from interfering with the distribution of political and electoral content posted by either Lula da Silva or Flávio Bolsonaro until the conclusion of the election’s second round, stating that failure to comply with the ruling would result in a daily fine of BRL 500,000 (USD 91,942). The decision came after Lula da Silva’s reelection campaign team denounced to the TSE that Meta repeatedly restricted the reach of publications linked to the government candidate and his supporters

On October 16, the newspaper Folha de S.Paulo reported that Meta employees acknowledged in internal communications that restrictions during the country's election hindered the Instagram accounts of Lula da Silva.

Meta acknowledged technical issues on its platforms on October 16, but said they were not the result of political bias. In an official statement, the company said the “ad account for Lula’s campaign was deactivated by mistake for just over an hour, and not for political reasons,” and that several of the reported problems were part of a “global” failure.

In his celebration speech, Lula da Silva promised to prioritize new regulations that ensure big digital media platforms are held accountable. He stated that during the recent election, he and his allies had to “overcome outside interference coming in through digital platforms,” and argued Brazil “cannot have monstrous companies earning billions, paying no taxes, and trying to steer” the country’s elections.

Social media and disinformation have played a central role in past elections in Brazil, as research shared by Harvard Kennedy School’s Misinformation Review, a scholarly publication, argues that in the 2022 election, “susceptibility to electoral misinformation is affected by factors such as political ideology, trust in the electoral process and democratic institutions, and information consumption, with those who participate in political groups in messaging apps being more likely to believe in electoral misinformation.”

As in 2022 but without the coup plot, the Bolsonaro family alleges electoral fraud. In a first letter shared after fleeing the country amid open investigations linking him to money laundering, Flávio Bolsonaro first declared himself “the elected president,” then deleted it and replaced it with a second version calling himself the rightful “leader” of Brazil. Bolsonaro argues in the text that he had to leave the country to prevent political persecution.

Although Flávio Bolsonaro insisted he would seek to annul the presidential election, his party later distanced itself from that position in a statement and chose to accept the official results, while still reporting irregularities during the electoral process.
Written by Civic Media Observatory, Samanta Azpurua
7bff3ad3cf63bad1: Last week, Anthropic introduced a new system prompt designed to stop its Claude models from re-creating specific, existing video games. While that move could help shield Anthropic from some liability, it's unlikely to slow much of the massive wave of AI-assisted game porting and copying that has emerged in recent months.

A social media user and AI decompilation enthusiast going by the name "chasm" was among the first to note the prompt change late last week, saying a new rule seemed to be added to the Claude Code prompt on or around October 27. That rule—included in a json file under the name "tengu_heron_brook"—reads as follows:
Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original.

XDA later independently verified that the new rule appears in version 2.1.314 of the Claude Code binary, which was released on October 30. XDA also reported that the "tengu_heron_brook" rule had been used for other purposes in earlier versions and that the Claude Opus 5.5 model specifically seemed to have its own distinct and independent instructions restricting game recreations as part of its system prompt bundle.
570887b3be63b924: Achille with Patroclo. Andre B da Cruz UNIPI, CC BYOn an Ethiopian plateau, a bull called Achille formed an unusual relationship with a male donkey named Patroclo. They were observed spending time together, licking and rubbing against one another, and repeatedly having penetrative sex. The animals’ names nod to Achilles and Patroclus, the Greek mythological figures whose bond has been debated for thousands of years: devoted friends – or lovers? A new study in the journal Current Biology asks something similar about Achille and Patroclo: why would two males of different species repeatedly choose each other as sexual partners when females of their own species are available? Perhaps the more interesting question is why we find their relationship so surprising. A chance find The researchers first noticed Achille and Patroclo while studying gelada monkeys in Ethiopia. Intrigued, they began observing the pair more closely. They recorded 51 mounting attempts, 34 of which involved penetration. Patroclo took an active role, presenting his hindquarters to Achille and initiating contact. Unlike another male donkey that Achille approached, Patroclo did not show obvious signs of trying to avoid him. The donkey and bull often showed affection towards each other immediately after mounting. This suggests that sex may help strengthen their bond. The researchers observed the pair in detail for just four days, so they cannot say how long the relationship lasted. Even so, the findings are unusual because the two animals are both male and belong to different species. Same-sex sexual behaviour has been reported in more than 1,500 animal species. A 2023 study documented it in 261 mammalian species and found that it was particularly associated with social species, suggesting a possible role in maintaining relationships and managing conflict. As a primatologist, I am not surprised by these findings. Bonobos, for example, are famous for their frequent sexual interactions, which occur in many combinations of partners. Female–female genital rubbing, for instance, is associated with affiliation and social bonding. Sexual interactions can also help manage social tensions. Same-sex sexual behaviour takes many forms. Male bottlenose dolphins mount one another and rub genitals in groups that cooperate to gain access to females, while female Japanese macaques form temporary sexual partnerships involving repeated mounting. Same-sex sexual behaviour may play a part in establishing status, settling disputes, forming friendships or sexual enjoyment. Sexual behaviour between different species is rarer, but it is not unheard of. Both male and female Japanese macaques, for example, mount sika deer. Unlike the apparently reciprocal relationship between Achille and Patroclo, these encounters do not necessarily involve mutual sexual interest. What makes Achille and Patroclo particularly interesting is that they combine sexual activity with apparent affection and a preference for each other. Evolutionary biologists have traditionally approached same-sex sexual behaviour as a puzzle. If natural selection favours traits that contribute to reproductive success, why should animals spend time and energy engaging in sexual behaviour that cannot directly produce offspring? Suggested explanations include mistaken identity, a lack of opposite-sex partners, or indiscriminate sexual behaviour with whichever individuals happen to be nearby. But all these explanations begin with an assumption that sexual behaviour between males and females is the default, and same-sex behaviour represents a departure from it. In a provocative 2019 paper, a team of researchers challenged this assumption. They proposed that the ancestors of sexually reproducing animals may have been relatively indiscriminate about the sex of their sexual partners. Rather than assuming that different-sex sexual behaviour came first, they suggested that the ability to distinguish between potential partners, and preferentially direct sexual behaviour towards the opposite sex, may have evolved later. Taking a queer perspective This is a brilliant example of how queer perspectives can enrich evolutionary biology. Queer approaches encourage scientists to examine how human assumptions about sex, gender and sexuality influence the questions we ask, the categories we use and the explanations we consider plausible. They do not require us to assign human sexual identities to animals. Observing same-sex sexual behaviour does not tell us that an animal is gay or establish a fixed sexual orientation. Instead, queer approaches encourage us to take the diversity of animal sexual behaviour seriously, without assuming what is normal or what needs explaining. The authors of the new study suggest that Achille and Patroclo’s sexual interactions may help maintain their social relationship. They also discuss the possible reproductive costs of spending time and energy on sexual activity that cannot result in offspring. But this framing raises another question. Why should we assume that sexual behaviour must contribute directly to reproduction to have evolutionary significance? Social relationships can influence survival, access to resources and future reproductive opportunities. Sexual behaviour that strengthens those relationships may therefore have adaptive benefits, even when it cannot directly produce offspring. Equally, sexual behaviour may arise from evolved mechanisms without every individual encounter necessarily providing an animal’s reproductive success. Achille and Patroclo cannot tell us why they choose one another. This short study can’t tell us what evolutionary purpose, if any, their relationship serves. But it does remind us that animal behaviour can be more diverse than our theories suggest. Perhaps the most important lesson is not that a bull and a donkey have formed an unusual sexual relationship. It is that understanding such relationships requires us to question our assumptions about what sex is, what it does, and what counts as natural. 4d3744be4285318b: Does it make sense to wait until late December to wrap up, like these California shoppers did in 2023? Mel Melcon/Los Angeles Times via Getty ImagesAmazon, Costco, Target, Walmart and other retailers begin their holiday sales as early as October. But there’s no need to rush to buy wool scarves, fuzzy throw blankets and the other holiday gifts on your list the second you spot some tinsel while shopping. As a finance professor who studies how people and companies make financial decisions, I can explain why the holiday shopping season starts so early: It can help retailers attract more customers while allowing cash-strapped shoppers to stretch purchases out across multiple paychecks. And, for people with deeper pockets, buying gifts early can help them avoid the stress that goes with last-minute shopping. Why retailers get such an early start Estimates for spending on holiday gifts, decor and the like between late 2026 and January 2027 range from about US$1 trillion to $1.7 trillion in the U.S. Some 29% of Americans plan to shell out their share of those large sums in early to mid-December this holiday season, while 17% will shop on Black Friday, the day after Thanksgiving, according to the Bank of America Holiday Spending survey. But many people like to shop for holiday gifts early – meaning before Halloween. Some do this out of necessity: They can’t afford to buy all the gifts they want to give unless they spread the cost over multiple paychecks. For others, it’s more of a preference. In a 2025 survey, about 54% of early shoppers said they want to manage their budgets gradually. In addition, 41% said they buy gifts early to avoid the stress associated with last-minute shopping. Retailers are adjusting by getting an early start on holiday sales and promoting seasonal items. By offering customers deals months before gift-giving commences, they can encourage even more people to join the early birds. And by launching promotions in October, they might secure sales that otherwise would go to their competitors later in the season. A longer selling season offers other advantages to retailers. It may ease pressure on their supply chain and logistics, since they can receive seasonal orders over three months instead of one or two. This minimizes shipping difficulties and lowers warehouse overhead costs. Building more time into the calendar to move seasonal inventory gives retailers more opportunities to sell those items. However, an earlier shopping season does not necessarily increase consumer spending overall. Some purchases may simply shift from December to October. Early birds could buy these Christmas decorations at a discount on Oct. 17, 2026. Smith Collection/Gado via Getty Images Beware of some early-shopping pitfalls To make sure that buying gifts long before the holidays occur is a wise move, early shoppers should read vendors’ fine print and research their return policies. Many big retailers are making their return policies more restrictive by shortening the length of time you can return purchases and adding return/restocking fees. In some cases, the deadline you face for returning an item could fall before the holidays. For example, Best Buy’s extended policy takes effect in 2026 only for purchases made on or after Oct. 30. Target similarly restricts its holiday-season returns window to items bought on or after Nov. 1. Amazon extended its holiday return policy in 2026. If you buy an item from Nov. 1 to Dec. 31, it can be returned until Jan. 31, 2027, except for Apple products, which can be returned until Jan. 15. Anyone who bought gifts beforehand will likely be subject to a standard 30-day return policy, which will expire long before Christmas. The timing of holiday shopping varies whether you buy gifts online or in brick-and-mortar stores. Anchiy/E+ via Getty Images When buying early makes financial sense Shopping early is smart when the costs of waiting could outweigh the potential benefits of spending your money earlier than otherwise necessary. For example, if a popular wool scarf that was priced at $100 in October is out of stock on Amazon by November, the supply is gone, but demand remains high. If you want to buy it for your mom and ensure it arrives in time, you may need to get it from other retailers. Maybe you can find the scarf on a website but is selling for $150. If time has run out, you might have to pay, say, $30 more for expedited shipping, bringing the total to $180. Clearly, you would have been better off buying it early on at a lower price. But that doesn’t mean you necessarily need to rush to buy a gift weeks or months ahead of when you’ll be placing it under a tree. First make sure that the price is in line with your expectations and what you’re willing to shell out. And you should do some comparison shopping to make sure other retailers aren’t charging less for the same or similar items. Remember, waiting to do your holiday shopping until the last minute can lead to unnecessary costs, like rush shipping fees. The key is to have a budget, recognize when the price is right, and know when to stop shopping. 6a62b628a03d80c8: From Ashraf Abdullah
Moaz Nair’s “Bedfellows and backstabbers on the winding road to Putrajaya” mistakes colourful language for a convincing explanation of Malaysian politics.

His argument rests on two questionable assumptions: that cooperation in the federal government requires permanent electoral allegiance, and that the next general election is guaranteed to produce a hung Parliament.
Neither should pass unchallenged.
The unity government emerged after GE15 in November 2022, when no coalition secured a parliamentary majority.

The 16th Yang di-Pertuan Agong urged political cooperation to resolve the impasse. Umno’s supreme council subsequently supported its participation in a unity government, specifying that it should not be led by Perikatan Nasional.

That context matters. Barisan Nasional (BN) helped establish a functioning administration following an inconclusive election. It did not merge with Pakatan Harapan (PH) or surrender its political identity.

Supporting an administration during a parliamentary term and deciding whom to contest alongside at the next election are distinct decisions. Describing that distinction as “backstabbing” requires more than metaphors about political bedrooms.

For accuracy, BN’s leadership has previously advocated extending cooperation into GE16. In June 2024, Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said BN would maintain cooperation with PH while contesting under its own symbol. That statement cannot simply be erased from the record.
But neither can it be treated as an irrevocable undertaking regardless of subsequent developments.
In January this year, Umno secretary-general Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki said the party had not decided whether cooperation with PH would continue at GE16.

More recently, Zahid reaffirmed BN’s commitment to the unity government until the end of the present Parliament. These statements underline why the governing commitment, and future electoral arrangements must be examined separately.

Zahid’s preference alone should not determine BN’s electoral future. As Umno president and BN chairman, he must secure support within his party and take into account the positions of other BN component parties.

Umno members, its decision-making bodies, MCA and MIC have interests and constituencies of their own. An arrangement affecting their survival requires collective backing. Leadership involves listening to those whom one leads. And lest we forget, BN makes decisions by consensus.
It must also involve listening to voters.
In my assessment, continued electoral cooperation with PH will be increasingly difficult to sell to voters frustrated by promises which remain unfulfilled.
PH campaigned on reform and better governance. Its supporters are entitled to judge the delivery against the expectations its leaders created.

BN cannot assume that those frustrations are somebody else’s problem. Sharing power also means sharing public scrutiny. Ignoring discontent to preserve an understanding between leaders could prove costly at the ballot box.

Resistance among many Malay voters to cooperation with DAP presents another challenge. This does not mean every Malay voter thinks alike, or that election results establish a single reason for voting.
They do, however, require BN to examine whether its present partnership helps recover traditional supporters or pushes them further away.

Nair’s treatment of Umno and PAS is heavy with derision. I find considerable venom in his descriptions of Umno and PAS in this particular article and in his past jottings, perhaps because both are Malay-based parties.
He makes little effort to understand the constituencies these parties represent. Their supporters deserve analysis rather than caricature.
The election evidence also deserves more attention than his confident prediction allows.

In Sabah’s November 2025 election, DAP failed to win any of the eight seats it contested. Its secretary-general Loke Siew Fook accepted responsibility. Much of the electoral benefit went to Warisan, illustrating that dissatisfaction with DAP need not translate automatically into support for MCA.
Nevertheless, the warning was unmistakable: established support cannot be taken for granted.
Johor delivered another forceful reminder. In the July 2026 state election, BN won 48 of 56 seats, including eight won by MCA. PH secured eight seats, six through DAP. PN failed to win a seat.
Those results demonstrate both BN’s renewed strength and the danger of assuming that any party possesses an unassailable electoral base.

An analysis by the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies, part of Nanyang Technological University (NTU), Singapore identified declining Chinese support for PH alongside weaker turnout in its urban strongholds.
Its estimates still placed most Chinese voters with PH but showed meaningful erosion. A party need not lose an entire community’s support to lose constituencies where the contest is close.
Some voters may choose MCA. Others may abstain. Neither response guarantees a particular national outcome, but both can alter electoral arithmetic.

Negeri Sembilan offers a different, equally relevant lesson. BN won 18 seats, PN seven and PH 11 in its August election. BN and PN therefore held 25 of the assembly’s 36 seats between them. Cooperation mattered to the resulting balance of power.

It would nevertheless be inaccurate to describe that result as proof of a wholesale Chinese rejection of PH. Bridget Welsh’s analysis estimated that Chinese support remained overwhelmingly with PH. The stronger argument concerns the combination of constituency results and cooperation between competing political forces.
Together, these elections challenge the notion that PH’s position is secure or that fragmentation must inevitably produce another hung Parliament.
My assessment is that an effective BN-PN electoral understanding could win a comfortable parliamentary majority.
Avoiding mutually damaging contests, consolidating overlapping support and recovering some non-Malay votes offer a credible route to that outcome.

That remains a forecast. Seat negotiations, candidates, turnout and the positions of Sabah and Sarawak parties will matter. But Nair cannot reasonably demand certainty from competing scenarios while presenting his own as guaranteed.

He should visit Melaka and take the pulse of the campaign. BN is contesting 23 seats and PN five. Zahid has publicly said BN would invite successful PN assemblymen into the administration if it forms the government. This is an openly stated political understanding, not a clandestine affair.
Melaka votes on Nov 14. Its verdict remains with the electorate.
Cooperation in government does not confer permanent ownership over a partner’s electoral choices.
Changed arrangements require explanation, but they do not automatically establish betrayal.
The road to Putrajaya may be winding but a hung Parliament, to my mind, is not a foregone conclusion, like Nair confidently puts it.
The writer is a former group managing editor of Media Prima Bhd’s Television Networks.

624e23d0cdf0ab77: Regina Barzilay, MIT’s School of Engineering Distinguished Professor of AI and Health, and James Collins, MIT’s Termeer Professor of Medical Engineering and Science, are the recipients of the 2026 Pritzker Prize for AI in Science Research Excellence.  The award recognizes their joint work in “pioneering AI-enabled antibiotic discovery, integrating deep learning, bioengineering, and experimental validation to identify novel antibacterial candidates against drug-resistant pathogens.”  Established in 2024 by the University of Chicago in partnership with Caltech, the Pritzker Prize for AI in Science Research Excellence recognizes contributions that jointly advance AI and the natural sciences or engineering. Barzilay and Collins, who are faculty co-leads of the Abdul Latif Jameel Clinic for Machine Learning in Health (Jameel Clinic) and affiliates of the MIT Schwarzman College of Computing and the MIT School of Engineering, published their first breakthrough paper together in 2020 with then-MIT postdoc and first author Jonathan Stokes (who worked in the Collins lab from 2017 to 2021) in Cell. The paper described the first artificial intelligence-discovered antibiotic, called halicin, named for the fictional AI system HAL 9000 in Stanley Kubrick’s 1968 film 2001: A Space Odyssey. A broad-spectrum antibiotic that was originally studied as a potential diabetes drug, halicin was identified by a deep learning model trained on 2,500 molecules. Upon testing, the research team found that halicin was able to kill antibiotic-resistant bacteria (i.e., “superbugs”) such as Clostridium difficile, Acinetobacter baumannii, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. A discovery process that once took years was completed in just a few weeks. Amidst the growing alarm around the global antimicrobial resistance crisis, the results demonstrated that AI could prove to be an effective tool for rapidly identifying new and effective antibiotics. Following halicin, Barzilay and Collins worked with Stokes (now an assistant professor at McMaster University) to use machine learning to identify abaucin in 2023, a narrow-spectrum antibiotic demonstrating effectiveness against A. baumannii, an antibiotic-resistant bacteria commonly found on hospital doorknobs and in the wounds of U.S. soldiers stationed in Iraq and Afghanistan. Notably, abaucin’s “narrow spectrum” efficacy against a single species of treatment-resistant bacteria is its main advantage, minimizing the likelihood of bacteria developing resistance and harming beneficial bacteria in the gut. “Historically, antibiotic discovery has depended on laborious, trial-and-error strategies,” says Collins. “This process is slow, costly, and unpredictable, often yielding few viable antibiotic candidates. With generative AI, we're now seeing a shift from AI being used as a tool for discovery to AI being used as a design tool. This shift opens new frontiers in antibiotic discovery that could bring us the next generation of lifesaving drugs.” In Barzilay’s view, “despite significant progress in molecular modeling, we are still in early stages of drug discovery. With AI, we can only automate parts of the pipeline, rather than totally transforming the discovery process. To make it happen, we need to work really hard to build realistic AI models of human biology.”
